```ts
    if (!claims.email_verified || !claims.email) return null;
    return (await db.users.findOne({ email: claims.email }))?.id ?? null;
  },
});

// src/app.ts
createApp({ auth: session, routes: [notes, sso], ... });
```

- **Routes.** `routes: [sso]` adds `GET /auth/login` and `GET /auth/callback` (public routes, listed in OpenAPI and `inferlo describe`). Link to `/auth/login?returnTo=/path` (or `sso.loginPath`); after the sign-in the browser goes to `returnTo`, which must be a path on the app (anything else becomes `/`, so the link cannot send users to another site). Register `<your app's URL>/auth/callback` as the redirect URI at the provider; when the app runs behind a proxy that changes the URL it sees, set `redirectUri` to that URL. `basePath: "/sso/okta"` moves both routes, to sign in with more than one provider.
- **What is checked.** The login route keeps a random state, nonce and PKCE verifier in a short-lived cookie (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, 10 minutes, a `__Host-` cookie on https). The callback accepts only the state that browser started, refuses an `iss` parameter naming another provider (RFC 9207) and an `error` from the provider, exchanges the code with the verifier and the client secret (`client_secret_basic`, or `client_secret_post` when the provider only takes that; public clients leave out `clientSecret`), then checks the ID token: its signature against the provider's keys (RS, PS, ES and EdDSA algorithms, keys found and cached as for [`jwt()`](#access-tokens-from-an-identity-provider-jwt)), `iss`, `aud` (the client id, and `azp` when there are several audiences), `exp`, `iat` and the nonce. The pending sign-in is used once. A failed check answers 400 IL3009 and signs nobody in.
- **The user.** `userId(claims, { db, req, tokens })` gets the ID token's claims (`sub`, `email`, `email_verified`, `name` and whatever the provider adds, such as `groups` or Entra ID's `tid`) and the provider's tokens (`tokens.accessToken` for its APIs; Inferlo does not store them). Return the id of the app's user to start the session, or `null` to refuse (403 IL3011). Trust `claims.email` only when `claims.email_verified` is true, or match users on `claims.sub` (store it on the user the first time).
- `scopes` (default `["openid", "email", "profile"]`) asks for more claims, such as `["email", "groups"]`; `openid` is always sent.
- The provider's OpenID configuration is loaded on the first sign-in and kept for 10 minutes; its endpoints must be https (plain http only on localhost). When the provider cannot be reached, or refuses the client id or secret, the sign-in answers 502 IL3010 with the cause in the log. Invalid options raise IL6047 at startup.
- **Signing out.** `routes: [sso]` also adds `POST /auth/logout` (`sso.logoutPath`). It ends the app's session, then sends the browser to the provider's `end_session_endpoint` to end the user's session there too (OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout), with the ID token as `id_token_hint`, the `client_id` and `post_logout_redirect_uri`. That URI is `postLogoutRedirectUri`, or the app's origin with `/`; register it at the provider. A signed-in browser must send the session's CSRF token, so other sites cannot sign users out:

  ```ts
  // In the route that renders the page:
  const csrf = await session.csrfToken(req);
  const form = `<form method="post" action="${sso.logoutPath}"><input type="hidden" name="_csrf" value="${csrf}"><button>Sign out</button></form>`;
  ```

  At sign-in the ID token is kept for this in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` cookie (`inferlo_oidc_id`, a `__Host-` cookie on https; ID tokens over 3500 bytes are not kept and the provider gets only the `client_id`). Only an ID token from this provider is sent back to it. For providers without an `end_session_endpoint` (Google, for one), or when the provider cannot be reached, the browser goes straight to `postLogoutRedirectUri`; the app's session has ended either way. `session.signOut(ctx)` in your own route still ends only the app's session.
- **Authorization parameters.** `authorizationParams` adds parameters to every sign-in at the provider: `{ prompt: "select_account" }` to always show the account picker, Google's `{ hd: "acme.com" }` to offer only accounts of a Google Workspace domain (still check `claims.hd` or the email domain in `userId`, as the parameter is only a hint), Entra ID's `{ domain_hint: "acme.com" }` to skip the home realm page, or a provider's own. The flow's own parameters (`state`, `nonce`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, ...) cannot be set (IL6047). Per sign-in, the login link takes `?loginHint=ada@acme.com` (sent as `login_hint`, to fill in the user's name at the provider) and `?prompt=login` (or `select_account`, `consent`, `none`, `create`; other values are ignored): `/auth/login?prompt=select_account&returnTo=/settings` for a "switch account" link.
- Tested against a local stand-in provider and against [oidc-provider](https://github.com/panva/node-oidc-provider) (a certified OpenID Connect server), 9.0.0 and the latest, in `test/oidc.test.ts` and `test/oidc-provider.test.ts`.

## Access tokens from an identity provider (JWT)

APIs whose users sign in with an identity provider (Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google, Keycloak, Clerk, WorkOS, Amazon Cognito, Supabase) receive the provider's access tokens as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `jwt()` checks them, with Web Crypto and no runtime dependency:

```ts
import { jwt } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

createApp({
  auth: jwt({
    issuer: "https://acme.eu.auth0.com/",          // the iss claim, exactly as the provider writes it
    audience: "https://api.acme.com",              // this API's identifier at the provider (the aud claim)
    user: (claims) => ({ id: claims.sub, email: claims.email as string, roles: (claims.permissions as string[]) ?? [] }),
  }),
});
```

- **What is checked.** The signature, against the issuer's signing keys: found through its OpenID configuration (`<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`, whose `issuer` must match) or given as `jwksUrl`. Then `iss` equals `issuer`, `aud` contains `audience` (a list accepts any of them), `exp` is required and not past, `nbf` and `iat` are not in the future, and `sub` is set, each with 60 seconds of clock tolerance (`clockToleranceSeconds`, at most 300). Any token that fails a check signs nobody in: private routes answer 401 IL3001 and public routes see no user. The reason is never sent to the client.
- **Algorithms.** RS256, RS384, RS512, PS256, PS384, PS512, ES256, ES384, ES512 and EdDSA (Ed25519) by default; `algorithms: ["RS256"]` narrows the list. The key must match the algorithm in the token (an RSA key never checks an HS256 token), `none` is never accepted, and tokens with a `crit` header are refused. Providers that sign with a shared secret (Supabase's legacy secret, some gateways) pass `secret` (at least 32 characters, from `config({ secrets })`) and get HS256 (`algorithms: ["HS256", "HS512"]` for more).
- **Keys.** Fetched on the first request, kept for 10 minutes (`cacheMs`), and fetched again when a token names a key id the set does not have (the provider rotated its keys), at most every 30 seconds, so random key ids cannot flood the provider. Key URLs must be https (plain http only on localhost). When the keys cannot be loaded and none are cached, requests that send a token answer 503 IL3008 (the provider or the network is down, the token may be fine); cached keys keep working while the provider is unreachable.
- **The user.** `user(claims, { db, req })` returns the app's user, or `null` to refuse the token (a blocked account, a missing scope). Without it, the user is `{ id: sub, email, name, roles }` with `roles` from a `roles` claim. Roles and permissions are in different claims per provider: Auth0 `permissions` (with RBAC on), Keycloak `realm_access.roles`, Entra ID `roles`, Okta `groups`; map them in `user`. Load your own user record there when you keep one: `user: async (claims, { db }) => db.users.findOne({ externalId: claims.sub })`.
- For tenant-scoped models, return `tenantId` from an organization claim (Auth0 `org_id`, Clerk `org_id`, WorkOS `org_id`) or pass `tenant`.
- To accept tokens and your own API keys, try the token first: `resolve: async (req, ctx) => (await tokens.resolve(req, ctx)) ?? apiKeys.resolve(req, ctx)` (see the end of [Cookie sessions](#cookie-sessions)).
- Invalid options raise IL6042 at startup: the audience is required, so tokens the provider issued for your other APIs are refused.

## Better Auth

An app that signs users in with [Better Auth](https://www.better-auth.com) (email and password, OAuth providers, two-factor, organizations, passkeys) uses its sessions as Inferlo's auth with `betterAuthSession(auth)` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/better-auth`. Better Auth keeps its own tables and endpoints; Inferlo routes get the signed-in user:

```ts
// src/auth.ts
import { betterAuth } from "better-auth";
import { admin } from "better-auth/plugins";
import { betterAuthSession } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/better-auth";
import { pool } from "./db.ts";
import { settings } from "./config.ts"; // BETTER_AUTH_SECRET: t.string().min(32), listed in secrets

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: pool,                       // the pg pool Inferlo uses too: postgres({ pool })
  secret: settings.BETTER_AUTH_SECRET,
  baseURL: settings.APP_URL,            // https://app.example.com
  emailAndPassword: { enabled: true },
  plugins: [admin()],                   // optional: user.role becomes the user's roles
});

export const session = betterAuthSession(auth, {
  user: ({ user }) => ({ id: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, roles: user.role ? user.role.split(",") : [] }),
});

// src/app.ts
createApp({ models, db: postgres({ pool }), routes, auth: session, middleware: [session.middleware] });
```

- `session.middleware` answers Better Auth's own endpoints (sign-up, sign-in, sign-out, OAuth callbacks, `get-session`) under its `basePath`, `/api/auth` by default, with `auth.handler`. Every other request goes on to the app. Inferlo's secure headers and request ids apply to Better Auth's answers too.
- `user({ user, session }, { db, req })` turns Better Auth's user and session into the app's user, or returns `null` to refuse the session (a blocked account). Without it, the user is `{ id, email, name, roles }` with `roles` from the admin plugin's comma-separated `user.role`. Apps that register their own user type pass `user`. For tenant-scoped models with Better Auth's organization plugin, return `tenantId: session.activeOrganizationId` (or pass `tenant`).
- **Cross-site protection.** Better Auth's cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, and Inferlo also refuses a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE that carries the session cookie when a browser sends it from another site: 403 IL3007 before the handler runs, also on public routes. Browsers mark every request with `Sec-Fetch-Site` or `Origin`, so the app's own pages pass without a token; clients that are not browsers (servers, CLIs, tests) send neither and pass. Pages on other origins of yours (an admin site) need `trustedOrigins: ["https://admin.example.com"]`; by default, Better Auth's own `trustedOrigins` list and the origin of its `baseURL` are trusted. Requests with an `Authorization` header (Better Auth's `bearer()` plugin, for mobile apps and scripts) are not checked, because browsers never add that header on their own.
- **Tables.** Better Auth's tables (`user`, `session`, `account`, `verification`) come from its own migrations (`npx @better-auth/cli migrate`, or `getMigrations(auth.options)` from `better-auth/db/migration` in code). `inferlo db migrate` never changes tables it did not create, and Better Auth's migrations never touch Inferlo's. Keep Better Auth's user id in Inferlo models as a plain field (`ownerId: t.string().index()`); read Better Auth's tables with `db.$sql('select name from "user" where id = $1', [id])`.
- Better Auth rate-limits its own endpoints in production; Inferlo's `rateLimit` applies to Inferlo routes. Shut down with `await app.close()`, then `await pool.end()`.
- Invalid arguments raise IL6041 at startup. A tested example is in `examples/with-better-auth`, tested with `better-auth` 1.6.0 and the latest Better Auth on the oldest supported and newest PostgreSQL.

## Auth.js

An app that signs users in with [Auth.js](https://authjs.dev) (`@auth/core`: OAuth providers, email links, credentials; used by Next.js, SvelteKit and Express apps) uses its sessions as Inferlo's auth with `authJsSession(Auth, config)` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/authjs`:

```ts
// src/auth.ts
import { Auth } from "@auth/core";
import GitHub from "@auth/core/providers/github";
import { authJsSession } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/authjs";
import { settings } from "./config.ts"; // AUTH_SECRET, AUTH_GITHUB_ID, AUTH_GITHUB_SECRET, listed in secrets

export const authConfig = {
  secret: settings.AUTH_SECRET,
  trustHost: true,                                  // or set AUTH_URL to the app's URL
  providers: [GitHub({ clientId: settings.AUTH_GITHUB_ID, clientSecret: settings.AUTH_GITHUB_SECRET })],
  callbacks: {
    // Auth.js leaves the user id out of the session; Inferlo needs it.
    session: ({ session, token }) => ({ ...session, user: { ...session.user, id: token.sub } }),
  },
};

export const session = authJsSession(Auth, authConfig);

// src/app.ts
createApp({ models, routes, auth: session, middleware: [session.middleware] });
```

- `session.middleware` answers Auth.js's own endpoints (`/auth/signin`, `/auth/callback/<provider>`, `/auth/signout`, `/auth/session`, `/auth/csrf`) under its `basePath`, `/auth` by default, with `Auth(req, config)`. Every other request goes on to the app.
- Inferlo reads the session the way Auth.js's framework adapters do, through its session endpoint, so JWT sessions (the default) and database sessions (with an adapter) both work. Without a session cookie, Auth.js is not called.
- `user(session, { db, req })` returns the app's user, or `null` to refuse the session. Without it, the user is `{ id, email, name, roles }` from `session.user`: `id` must be in the session (add it in `callbacks.session` as above; with database sessions, `({ session, user }) => ({ ...session, user: { ...session.user, id: user.id } })`), or the request answers 500 IL6044 with that fix in the log. `roles` come from `session.user.roles` when your callbacks add them.
- **Cross-site protection.** As with Better Auth, a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE that carries the Auth.js session cookie from another site is refused with 403 IL3007 (checked with `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Origin`). Other origins of yours go in `trustedOrigins: ["https://admin.example.com"]`. Auth.js's own endpoints keep their own CSRF token.
- Invalid arguments raise IL6043 at startup. Tested with `@auth/core` 0.41.0 and the latest Auth.js in `test/authjs.test.ts`. Auth.js is now maintained by the Better Auth team, which recommends Better Auth for new projects; both work with Inferlo.

## Passport.js

An Express app that signs users in with [Passport.js](https://www.passportjs.org) (local, OAuth, SAML and its other strategies, with `express-session`) mounts its Inferlo app with `toNodeHandler` and uses `passportSession()` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/passport` as the app's auth. Passport's strategies, `serializeUser` and `deserializeUser` stay as they are; Inferlo routes get the user Passport put on `req.user`:

```ts
// src/app.ts
import { createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { passportSession } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/passport";

export const app = createApp({
  models,
  routes,
  auth: passportSession({ user: (account: Account) => ({ id: account.id, email: account.email, name: account.displayName, roles: account.roles }) }),
});

// src/server.ts: the existing Express app
server.use(session({ secret: settings.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false, saveUninitialized: false }));
server.use(passport.session());                 // Passport puts the signed-in user on req.user
server.use("/api", toNodeHandler(app));         // after Passport, so Inferlo routes see that user
```

- `user(passportUser, { db, req, nodeRequest })` returns the app's user, or `null` to refuse it (a blocked account). Without it, the user is `{ id, email, name, roles }` from Passport's user: `id` (a number becomes a string), `name` from `name` or `displayName`, and `roles` from `roles`. A Passport user without an id answers 500 IL6046 with the fix in the log.
- Strategies without a session (`passport.authenticate("bearer", { session: false })` in front of `toNodeHandler`) work the same way: whatever Passport puts on `req.user` signs the request in.
- **Cross-site protection.** As with Better Auth and Auth.js, a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE whose login comes from the `express-session` cookie is refused with 403 IL3007 when a browser sends it from another site (checked with `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Origin`). Other origins of yours go in `trustedOrigins: ["https://admin.example.com"]`. Logins from a strategy with `session: false` are not checked: no cookie signs them in.
- Inferlo reads `req.user` from the Node.js request the app was given, so the app must run through `toNodeHandler` (or `fromNodeRequest`) after `passport.session()`. Through `app.listen()` or `app.fetch()` there is no Express request, and private routes answer 500 IL6046 with that fix. WebSocket upgrades do not pass through Express middleware, so `route.ws` routes see no Passport user.
- Invalid options raise IL6045 at startup. Tested with Passport 0.6.0 (the first release that regenerates the session at login) and the latest Passport, on Express 4 and 5, in `test/passport.test.ts`.


```ts
import { bearer, hashToken, createToken } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

createApp({
  auth: bearer(async (token, { db }) => {
    const key = await db.api_keys.findOne({ hash: await hashToken(token) });
    if (!key) return null;
    const user = await db.users.find(key.userId);
    return user && { id: user.id, email: user.email, name: user.name, roles: [user.role] };
  }),
});

// Issuing a key: show the token once, store only the hash.
const token = createToken("live");
await db.api_keys.insert({ userId, hash: await hashToken(token) });
```

`bearer()` reads `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and falls back to an `x-api-key` header.

## Passwords

```ts
import { hashPassword, verifyPassword } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

const stored = await hashPassword(password);      // PBKDF2-SHA256, 210,000 iterations
const ok = await verifyPassword(password, stored);
```

These use Web Crypto, so they run on Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes.

## The user type

Declare your user type once (see [database](database.md#register-your-models-once)) and `ctx.user` is typed in every handler.

In multi-tenant apps, give the user a `tenantId` (or pass `tenant: (user) => user.orgId` to `bearer`, `sessions` or `auth`): `ctx.db` then filters and stamps tenant-scoped models with it. See [multi-tenancy](database.md#multi-tenancy).

---

# AI

Inferlo's AI module gives every route one API for every model provider, with aliases, automatic fallback, typed structured output, streaming, embeddings, usage tracking and budgets.

## Configure

```ts
import { createApp, env, anthropic, openai, gemini, ollama, openaiCompatible } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

createApp({
  ai: {
    providers: {
      anthropic: anthropic({ apiKey: env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") }),
      openai: openai({ apiKey: env("OPENAI_API_KEY") }),
      local: ollama(),
      deepseek: openaiCompatible({ name: "deepseek", baseURL: "https://api.deepseek.com/v1", apiKey: env("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY") }),
    },
    // Aliases: routes use "fast" and "smart", never provider model ids.
    // A list is a fallback order: if the first fails with a timeout, 429 or 5xx, the next is tried.
    models: {
      fast: ["anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5", "openai:gpt-5-mini"],
      smart: ["anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", "openai:gpt-5"],
      embed: "openai:text-embedding-3-small",
    },
    // Optional: USD per million tokens, for cost tracking. Inferlo ships no prices because they change.
    pricing: { "anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5": { input: 1, output: 5 } },
    onUsage: (usage) => console.log(usage),
    allow: async ({ for: userId }) => (await credits(userId)) > 0,
  },
});
```

### Any Vercel AI SDK provider

`aiSdk(provider)` turns any [Vercel AI SDK](https://ai-sdk.dev) provider into an Inferlo provider, so the providers Inferlo has no adapter of its own for (Mistral, Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Google Vertex AI, Groq, xAI, Cohere, the AI Gateway and the others) work with aliases, fallback, structured output, tools, streaming, embeddings, usage tracking, budgets and tracing:

```ts
import { aiSdk, createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { createMistral } from "@ai-sdk/mistral";
import { bedrock } from "@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock";

createApp({
  ai: {
    providers: {
      mistral: aiSdk(createMistral({ apiKey: settings.MISTRAL_API_KEY })),
      bedrock: aiSdk(bedrock),
    },
    models: {
      fast: ["mistral:mistral-small-latest", "bedrock:anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0"],
      embed: "mistral:mistral-embed",
    },
  },
});
```

- Pass the **provider** (what `createMistral()` returns, or the default `mistral` instance), not a model: the part after the colon in `"mistral:mistral-small-latest"` is the model id Inferlo asks the provider for, as with every other provider. To use models you built yourself (for example with `wrapLanguageModel` middleware), group them with `customProvider({ languageModels: { ... }, embeddingModels: { ... } })` from `ai` and pass that.
- Works with providers made for `ai` 5, 6 and 7 (`@ai-sdk/*` 2.0 and later: language model specifications v2, v3 and v4). Inferlo does not depend on the AI SDK; install the provider packages you use. An older provider, or anything that is not a provider, raises IL5029.
- Errors of the AI SDK (`APICallError`) become IL5006 with the HTTP status, so 429, 5xx and network errors move on to the next model of an alias like any other provider. Embeddings are sent in batches of the model's `maxEmbeddingsPerCall`.
- The provider name in errors and traces is the AI SDK's own (`mistral`); `aiSdk(provider, { name: "eu-mistral" })` sets another.
- `ai.stream` streams text; tool calls are available with `ai.generate`, as with every provider.

## Use it without createApp

The AI module also works on its own, in any framework (Express, Hono, Fastify, NestJS, Next.js route handlers), a script or a queue worker. Import it from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai`, which never loads the router, database or jobs code:

```ts
import { createAI, anthropic, openai, env, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai";

export const ai = createAI({
  providers: {
    anthropic: anthropic({ apiKey: env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") }),
    openai: openai({ apiKey: env("OPENAI_API_KEY") }),
  },
  models: { fast: ["anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5", "openai:gpt-5-mini"], embed: "openai:text-embedding-3-small" },
  onUsage: (usage) => console.log(usage),
});

const { object } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  prompt: "Classify: the export button does nothing",
  output: t.object({ label: t.enum(["bug", "feature", "question"]) }),
  for: userId,
});
```

`createAI` takes the same options as `createApp({ ai })`, and `ai` has the same `generate`, `stream`, `embed` and `aliases` as `ctx.ai` in a route handler. The entry point also exports the providers, `mockProvider` for tests, `t` and `toJSONSchema` for structured output, `tool` for [function tools](#tools-let-the-model-call-your-functions), `env`, `InferloError`, `httpError` and the types (`AI`, `AIConfig`, `Usage`, `Message`, `Provider`, `ToolDef`, ...). Tools made from routes need a route handler (IL5009); function tools work anywhere.

`openaiCompatible()` works with any Chat Completions server: OpenAI, DeepSeek, Qwen (DashScope), Groq, Together, OpenRouter, vLLM, LM Studio and others.

## Generate text

```ts
const { text, usage } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  system: "You are a support assistant.",
  prompt: "Reply to: my order is late",
  for: user.id,
});
```

## Images (vision)

Pass images with the prompt to any vision model (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, and OpenAI-compatible servers such as Ollama with a vision model):

```ts
const { text } = await ai.generate({
  model: "fast",
  prompt: "What is wrong in this screenshot?",
  images: [{ url: "https://example.com/screenshot.png" }],
  for: user.id,
});

// Base64 data, for example from an upload: no data: prefix, plus the media type.
await ai.generate({ prompt: "Read the receipt total", images: [{ base64: data, mediaType: "image/jpeg" }], output: Receipt });
```

- An image is `{ url }` (`https://`, `http://` or a `data:image/...;base64,` URL) or `{ base64, mediaType }`. Media types: `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/gif`, `image/webp`.
- In a conversation, put images on user messages: `messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Here is the receipt", images: [...] }]`.
- Remote URLs are passed to the provider as they are, and the provider downloads them; Inferlo never fetches them. If a provider cannot download a URL, send base64 instead.
- Works with `ai.stream`, `output` and `tools` too. Invalid images raise IL5012 before any model is called.
- In tests, `mockProvider` receives the images on `request.messages[i].images`.

## Structured output

Pass a schema and get typed, validated data back:

```ts
const Triage = t.object({
  priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]),
  summary: t.string().max(300).describe("One sentence for the agent"),
});

const { object } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: ticket.body, output: Triage });
object.priority; // "low" | "normal" | "urgent"
```

Inferlo sends the JSON Schema to the model, extracts the JSON (tolerating code fences), validates it, and if it does not match, asks the model once to fix it, quoting the exact problems. If it still fails you get IL5002. Model fields can be reused directly: `priority: Ticket.fields.priority`.

### Zod, Valibot and ArkType schemas

Apps that already describe their data with Zod, Valibot or ArkType (often when `@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai` runs inside Express, NestJS, Fastify or Next.js) can pass those schemas as `output`, and as a [tool's](#tools-let-the-model-call-your-functions) `input`. Any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) that also implements Standard JSON Schema works:

```ts
import { createAI } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai";
import { z } from "zod";

const Triage = z.object({
  priority: z.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]),
  summary: z.string().max(300).describe("One sentence for the agent"),
});

const { object } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: ticket.body, output: Triage });
object.priority; // "low" | "normal" | "urgent", typed by Zod
```

| Library | Pass | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| Zod | `z.object({ ... })` | zod 4.2 or later |
| ArkType | `type({ ... })` | arktype 2.1.28 or later |
| Valibot | `toStandardJsonSchema(v.object({ ... }))` from `@valibot/to-json-schema` | `@valibot/to-json-schema` 1.5 or later (a plain Valibot schema has no JSON Schema) |

- The model is shown the library's own JSON Schema (`"~standard".jsonSchema.input`), and its answer is validated by the library, so transforms and defaults apply and `object` has the library's output type. Mismatches are sent back to the model with the library's messages, as with `t.*` schemas.
- The schema must be expressible as JSON Schema: no `z.date()`, functions or input-side transforms. A schema that is not one, or that has no JSON Schema, raises IL5032 before any model is called.
- Inside an Inferlo app, keep using `t.*` schemas for routes, models and jobs; Standard Schema support is for the AI module only, so existing schemas can be reused there.

## Tools: let the model call your functions

Make a tool from a plain function with `tool(name, { description, input }).handle(fn)` and pass it in `tools`. Function tools work everywhere: with `createAI` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai` in any framework, and with `ctx.ai` in a route handler, next to route tools.

```ts
import { createAI, tool, t, httpError } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai";

export const getWeather = tool("getWeather", {
  description: "Current weather for a city",
  input: t.object({ city: t.string(), unit: t.enum(["c", "f"]).default("c") }),
}).handle(async ({ input, signal }) => {
  const weather = await weatherApi(input.city, input.unit, { signal });
  if (!weather) throw httpError(404, `No weather for ${input.city}.`);
  return weather;
});

const { text, steps } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: "Do I need an umbrella in Oslo?", tools: [getWeather] });
```

- **Input is validated.** The model's arguments are checked against `input` (defaults applied) before your function runs. `input` is a `t.object({ ... })`, or an object schema from Zod, ArkType or Valibot (see [Zod, Valibot and ArkType schemas](#zod-valibot-and-arktype-schemas)): `tool("fileTicket", { description, input: z.object({ title: z.string() }) })`. Invalid arguments go back to the model as a failed tool result with status 422 and IL1001, so it can correct itself.
- **Output** is any JSON value, sent to the model as JSON, or a string, sent as it is. `steps[i].toolCalls` has the `output` with status 200.
- **Errors.** Throw `httpError(404, "...")` (or `notFound`, `forbidden`, any `InferloError` with a status below 500) to send a failed tool result to the model. Any other error is not hidden: `ai.generate` rejects with it, after reporting the usage so far.
- **Names** are letters, digits, `_` and `-` (the provider limit), and must be unique in one call. Invalid definitions raise IL5013.
- `signal` is the `ai.generate` call's `signal`, so long tools stop with the call.
- Step limit, usage per step, budgets and fallback work as for route tools below.

## Tools: let the model call your routes

Pass routes as `tools` and the model can call them while it works out its answer. Each tool call runs as an HTTP request to the route **as the current user**: the route's `auth`, roles and schema validation apply exactly as they do for any other client, so a model can never do more than the user could.

```ts
import { route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { createTicket, getTicket, listTickets } from "./tickets.ts";

export const assistant = route
  .post("/assistant", { body: t.object({ message: t.string().max(4000) }) })
  .handle(async ({ ai, body, user }) => {
    const { text, steps, usage } = await ai.generate({
      model: "smart",
      system: "You help users manage their support tickets.",
      prompt: body.message,
      tools: [createTicket, getTicket, listTickets],
      maxSteps: 5,
      for: user.id,
    });
    return { reply: text, toolCalls: steps.flatMap((s) => s.toolCalls.map((c) => c.name)), cost: usage.cost };
  });
```

- **Names and arguments** come from the route: the tool name is the route's export name (`createTicket`, or `tool: { name }`), the description is `tool.description`, `description` or `summary`, and the arguments are the route's `params`, `query` and `body` fields in one JSON Schema (the same tool the MCP server shows). Routes do not need `tool: true` to be used here; that option only controls the MCP server.
- **Errors go back to the model.** A 403, 404 or 422 from the route (or an unknown tool name) is sent to the model as a failed tool result, so it can correct itself.
- **Step limit.** `maxSteps` (default 5) is the most model calls, tool rounds plus the final answer. A model still calling tools at the limit raises IL5010.
- **Usage per step.** `steps` lists every model call with its `text`, `toolCalls` (`name`, `input`, `status`, `output`, `isError`) and `usage`; `usage` has the totals and is reported to `onUsage` once. `allow` is checked again before every model call that follows tool calls, so budgets stop a long run.
- **Fallback.** Once a tool has run, Inferlo does not retry on the next model in the alias (that would run the tools again); the call fails with IL5006.
- **Structured output** works with tools: pass `output` and the final answer is validated as usual.
- Works with Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and OpenAI-compatible servers whose models support tool calling. Route tools only work through `ctx.ai` inside a route handler (IL5009), and must be routes registered in `createApp` (IL5011); function tools work anywhere. Streaming with tools is not supported yet.

In tests, a `mockProvider` can return tool calls:

```ts
mockProvider({
  respond: (r) => (r.messages.at(-1)!.role === "tool" ? "Created it." : { toolCalls: [{ name: "createTicket", input: { title: "Printer on fire" } }] }),
});
```

## Streaming

```ts
export const chat = route
  .post("/chat", { body: t.object({ message: t.string().max(4000) }) })
  .handle(({ body, ai, user }) => ai.stream({ model: "fast", prompt: body.message, for: user.id }).toResponse());
```

`toResponse()` sends server-sent events: `text` events with JSON-encoded chunks, then a `done` event with usage. You can also iterate: `for await (const chunk of ai.stream(...))`, or `await stream.text()`.

### Chat UIs with the Vercel AI SDK (useChat)

`toResponse({ format: "ai-sdk" })` answers with the AI SDK UI message stream protocol, so `useChat` from `@ai-sdk/react` (or `@ai-sdk/vue`, `@ai-sdk/svelte`) talks to an Inferlo route directly. `uiChatBody` validates the body `useChat` sends, and `fromUIMessages` turns its messages into model messages:

```ts
import { fromUIMessages, route, uiChatBody } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const chat = route
  .post("/api/chat", { body: uiChatBody, rateLimit: { max: 30, per: "minute" } })
  .handle(({ body, ai, user }) =>
    ai.stream({ model: "fast", messages: fromUIMessages(body.messages), for: user.id }).toResponse({ format: "ai-sdk" }),
  );
```

```tsx
// In the browser (React). useChat posts to /api/chat by default.
import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";

const { messages, sendMessage, status } = useChat();
```

- **Body.** `uiChatBody` accepts what `useChat` sends (`{ id, messages, trigger, ... }`) and keeps each message's `role` (`system`, `user` or `assistant`) and its parts' `type` and `text`; ids, metadata and other fields are dropped. It allows 1 to 500 messages, 100 parts per message and 100,000 characters per text part. Combine it with a route's `rateLimit` and the AI module's budgets.
- **Messages.** `fromUIMessages(messages)` joins the text parts of each message and leaves out other parts (files, reasoning, tool calls, data parts); messages without text are dropped. Add your own system message in front: `messages: [{ role: "system", content: "..." }, ...fromUIMessages(body.messages)]`. A client can send any role, including `system`, so filter with `.filter((m) => m.role !== "system")` when callers must not change your instructions.
- **Stream.** The answer is one text part: `start`, `text-start`, `text-delta` chunks, `text-end`, `finish`, then `[DONE]`, with the `x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1` header. If the model call fails, the stream ends with an `error` chunk that carries only the error code (`The model call failed (IL5006).`); details stay in your logs. Usage is recorded on the server (`onUsage`, budgets), not sent to the browser.
- **Auth.** The route is private by default: `useChat({ transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "/api/chat", headers: { authorization: "Bearer " + token } }) })` sends a token, and cookie sessions work without extra options.
- **Versions.** Tested with the `ai` package 5.0.0 (the first release with this protocol) and the latest release, through its `DefaultChatTransport`, the transport `useChat` uses. Nothing from the `ai` package is loaded by Inferlo.
- An unknown `format` raises IL5027.

## Embeddings

```ts
const { embeddings } = await ai.embed({ input: ["first text", "second text"] });   // uses the "embed" alias
cosineSimilarity(embeddings[0], embeddings[1]);
```

## Usage and budgets

Every call reports a `Usage` record (`requested`, `model` that answered, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cost`, `for`, `kind`, `durationMs`) to `onUsage`. Store it to bill customers. When `for` is set, `allow` is called first; returning false raises IL5004 (HTTP 402).

## Tracing

With `createApp({ tracing: { api: otel } })` (or `createAI({ ..., tracing: { api: otel } })` on its own), every call gets an OpenTelemetry span with the provider, the model that answered, tokens and cost; prompts and answers are never recorded. See [Observability, "AI calls"](observability.md#ai-calls).

## Testing

```ts
import { mockProvider } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

ai: { providers: { mock: mockProvider({ respond: () => '{"priority":"urgent","summary":"Down"}' }) }, models: { fast: "mock:test" } }
```

---

# Background jobs

Jobs run work after the response is sent, with retries: sending email, calling a slow AI model, processing an upload. A job is a plain value, like a route.

```ts
// src/jobs.ts
import { job, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const summarizeNote = job("summarize-note", {
  input: t.object({ noteId: t.uuid() }),
  retries: 3,              // default 3: up to 4 runs in total
  summary: "Write an AI summary of a note",
}).handle(async ({ input, db, ai, attempt }) => {
  const note = await db.notes.get(input.noteId);
  const { text } = await ai.generate({ model: "fast", prompt: `Summarize:\n\n${note.body}`, for: note.ownerId });
  await db.notes.update(note.id, { summary: text });
});
```

Register jobs in `createApp`, like routes:

```ts
import * as jobs from "./jobs.ts";

export const app = createApp({ models, routes: [notes], jobs: [jobs], ... });
```

## Enqueue

From a route handler, with `ctx.jobs`:

```ts
export const createNote = route
  .post("/notes", { body: Note.pick("title", "body") })
  .handle(async ({ body, user, db, jobs, status }) => {
    const note = await db.notes.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id });
    await jobs.enqueue(summarizeNote, { noteId: note.id });
    status(201);
    return note;
  });
```

Anywhere else, with `app.jobs.enqueue(job, input)`.

- Pass the job itself, not its name, so the input is typed and checked by TypeScript.
- The input is validated against the job's schema when it is enqueued (IL1001 if it does not match) and again when the job runs. It is stored as JSON, so pass ids, not rows: dates arrive as ISO strings and `t.date()` turns them back into `Date`.
- `enqueue(job, input, { runAt: new Date(Date.now() + 60_000) })` runs the job no earlier than `runAt`.
- **Tenants** (multi-tenant apps, see [multi-tenancy](database.md#multi-tenancy)): a job queued by a request whose user has a tenant gets that tenant, and so do the jobs of events it publishes and the follow-ups a job queues. The job's `ctx.db` is scoped to it and `ctx.tenantId` names it. From `app.jobs`, pass it: `enqueue(job, input, { tenantId: "acme" })`; `{ tenantId: null }` queues a job without a tenant. The tenant is stored with the job in every store (`memory`, `database`, `redis`) and travels with events between services.
- `enqueue` returns the job record: `{ id, name, input, status, attempts, maxAttempts, runAt, lastError?, tenantId?, createdAt, updatedAt }`. `app.jobs.get(id)` reads it again. `status` is `"pending"`, `"running"`, `"done"` or `"failed"`.

## Handlers

The handler receives `{ input, db, ai, jobs, events, cache, audit, id, attempt, tenantId }` (`cache` is the app cache, see [Caching](caching.md)). `attempt` is 1 on the first run. `jobs.enqueue` inside a job queues follow-up jobs. There is no signed-in user: pass the user id in the input and use `for: userId` on AI calls. `ai.generate({ tools })` only works in route handlers (IL5009).

Throw to fail an attempt. A failed job runs again after 10 seconds, then 20, 40, and so on (at most one hour between attempts), until its retries are used up; then its status is `"failed"` and the error is logged. `lastError` holds the last error message. Make handlers safe to run twice: a retry runs the whole handler again.

## Running jobs

```ts
// src/server.ts
const server = await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
app.jobs.start();                      // runs due jobs every second (pollMs: 1000)
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close());   // stops the worker, waits for the running job
```

New projects do this in `src/server.ts`. `app.close()` stops every worker started with `app.jobs.start()` and waits for its running job, together with in-flight requests, then closes the server and the database (see [graceful shutdown](deploy.md#graceful-shutdown)). To stop only the jobs, keep the worker and call `await worker.stop()`.

To run jobs in separate processes, keep them in the database (below) and start `inferlo worker` (`npm run worker` in new projects). It runs `app.jobs.start()` and, on SIGTERM or Ctrl+C, waits for the running job before it exits. Web servers and workers share the queue, so you can run jobs in both or only in workers. See [CLI](cli.md#inferlo-worker).

## Cron

`cron(schedule, job)` queues a job on a schedule. Export it next to the job; registering the module registers both:

```ts
// src/jobs.ts
import { cron, job, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const deleteOldSessions = job("delete-old-sessions", { input: t.object({}) }).handle(async ({ db }) => {
  await db.sessions.deleteMany({ expiresAt: { lt: new Date() } });
});

export const nightly = cron("0 3 * * *", deleteOldSessions);   // every day at 03:00 UTC
```

- The schedule has five fields, `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, always in UTC: numbers, `*`, ranges (`1-5`), lists (`1,15`), steps (`*/15`, `5/20`) and names (`jan`, `mon`). Sunday is `0` or `7`. When both day fields are set, either one matching is enough, as in standard cron. Invalid schedules raise IL6013 when the module loads.
- `"*/15 * * * *"` every 15 minutes, `"0 * * * *"` every hour, `"30 3 * * 1-5"` at 03:30 on weekdays, `"0 0 1 * *"` on the first of each month.
- The job runs with the input `{}`, so its schema must accept it (IL6013 otherwise). Read what it needs from the database.
- Crons run while a worker runs: `app.jobs.start()` or `inferlo worker`. At each tick the job is queued and then runs like any other job, with its retries. Ticks are only queued after the worker started, and if the worker was paused past several ticks, only the latest one is queued.
- Each tick gets a fixed job id, so with the database queue every instance can run the schedule and the job is still queued once per tick.
- `cron.next(date)` returns the first tick after a date, and `app.jobs.crons` lists the crons. To test the work itself, enqueue the job: `await app.jobs.enqueue(deleteOldSessions, {})`, then `await app.jobs.runDue()`.

## Events

An event says that something happened (`order.paid`, `note.deleted`). The code that publishes it does not know who reacts; jobs subscribe to it with `on(event, job)`. Each subscribed job runs in the background with the event's payload, with its own retries.

```ts
// src/events.ts
import { event, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const orderPaid = event("order.paid", {
  payload: t.object({ orderId: t.uuid(), amount: t.int().min(0) }),
  summary: "An order was paid",   // shown in describe
});
```

```ts
// src/jobs.ts
import { job, on } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { orderPaid } from "./events.ts";

export const sendReceipt = job("send-receipt", { input: orderPaid.payload }).handle(async ({ input, db }) => { ... });
export const addPoints = job("add-points", { input: orderPaid.payload }).handle(async ({ input, db }) => { ... });

export const subscriptions = [on(orderPaid, sendReceipt), on(orderPaid, addPoints)];
```

```ts
// in a route handler (or a job, with ctx.events), after the change is saved
await ctx.events.publish(orderPaid, { orderId: order.id, amount: order.total });
```

- `events.publish(event, payload)` validates the payload (a `ValidationError`, 422 in a route) and queues every job subscribed to the event (with a transport, see below, every service queues its own), then returns `{ id, name, publishedAt, jobs }` (the queued job ids). The jobs run like any job: in `app.jobs.start()` or `inferlo worker`, with retries, in the memory, database or Redis queue, and in `app.jobs.runDue()` in tests. Publishing an event no job subscribes to is fine: it queues nothing.
- `app.events.publish(...)` publishes from scripts and tests. In jobs, `ctx.events` is the same.
- Registering `on(event, job)` (in `createApp({ jobs })` or a module's `jobs`) registers its job too. Use the event's payload as the job's input (`input: orderPaid.payload`); a job whose input is an object with fewer fields gets only those fields, and a job that requires a field the payload does not have raises IL6032, as does an invalid event name, two different events with the same name, or the same job subscribed twice to one event.
- Each queued job's id is derived from the event id and the job name, so publishing the same event id again queues nothing new: pass `{ id }` to make publishing idempotent, for example with the id of the row the event comes from (`events.publish(orderPaid, payload, { id: order.id })`). Handlers should still be idempotent, since a job can run again after a crash.
- With `createApp({ tracing })`, the subscribed jobs continue the trace of the request that published the event.
- `app.events.list` and `app.events.subscriptions` list the events and subscriptions, and `inferlo describe` shows each event with its payload schema and jobs.

### Between services

With `createApp({ events: { transport } })`, published events go to every service with an `on(event, job)` subscription for them, through a message broker. Redis Streams is built in:

```ts
// in each service: shop (publishes order.paid), billing and mail (subscribe to it)
const redis = await createClient({ url: settings.REDIS_URL }).connect();   // from the redis package

export const app = createApp({
  name: "billing",                     // also the consumer group: one per service
  redis,
  jobs: [jobs],                        // on(orderPaid, createInvoice)
  events: { transport: "redis" },
});
```

- Share the event definitions between services (a small package or a shared folder), so publisher and subscribers check payloads with the same schema.
- `events.publish(event, payload)` validates the payload and sends it; it does not queue jobs itself. Every service, the publishing one too, queues the jobs of its own subscriptions when it receives the event. `publish` still returns the ids those jobs will have in this app.
- Services receive events while a worker runs (`app.jobs.start()` or `inferlo worker`), on every poll before due jobs run. `await app.events.receive()` receives the waiting events once (scripts and tests) and returns how many.
- Delivery is at least once: an event is acknowledged after its jobs are queued, and an event an instance read but did not acknowledge (it crashed) is delivered again after 30 seconds. Since job ids come from the event id, a repeated delivery queues nothing new.
- Each service gets each event once, however many instances it runs: the instances of one service (same `name`) share its events. That is why the Redis transport needs `createApp({ name })` (IL6033 without it).
- A service only gets the events published after it first received from the transport (its worker's first poll creates its consumer group), so start subscribers before you rely on their events.
- A received event whose payload does not match the subscriber's schema is logged with IL6034 (without the payload) and dropped, since delivering it again cannot help. Change payloads compatibly: add optional fields, and remove a field only after every subscriber stopped requiring it.
- With `createApp({ tracing })`, the trace of the publishing request travels with the event, so the subscribed jobs in other services are part of the same trace.
- `app.events.transport` is `"redis"` (or your transport's name), shown as `eventTransport` in `inferlo describe`. An unknown transport or option raises IL6033; `transport: "redis"` without `createApp({ redis })` raises IL6031.

Keys, trimming and the details of the Redis transport are in [Redis, "Events"](redis.md#events). Another broker can be used by passing an object that implements `EventTransport` (`{ name, send(message), receive(names, deliver) }`). NATS JetStream and RabbitMQ have transports in their own entry points (below); a Kafka transport is planned.

### NATS JetStream

Services that already run NATS use `natsEventTransport` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/nats` (needs `@nats-io/jetstream` 3 and a NATS connection, for example from `@nats-io/transport-node`; the server needs JetStream, `nats-server -js`, version 2.11 or later):

```ts
import { connect } from "@nats-io/transport-node";
import { natsEventTransport } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/nats";

const nc = await connect({ servers: settings.NATS_URL });

export const app = createApp({
  name: "billing",
  jobs: [jobs],                        // on(orderPaid, createInvoice)
  events: { transport: natsEventTransport(nc, { service: "billing" }) },
});
```

- Events are published to the JetStream stream `INFERLO_EVENTS` (subjects `inferlo.events.<event name>`), created on first use with a 7-day `maxAgeMs` and a 2-minute duplicate window. The stream is shared by every service; create it yourself (same name and subjects) to choose replicas, storage or limits.
- Each service reads each event it subscribes to through its own durable pull consumer, `inferlo-<service>-<event name with "_" for ".">`, created at its first read with "deliver new". Instances of one service share its consumers, so each service gets each event once. Pass the app's name as `service`.
- An event is acknowledged after its jobs are queued. One whose delivery fails, or that an instance read without acknowledging (it stopped), is delivered again after `staleAfterMs` (default 30000). Publishing sets `Nats-Msg-Id` to the event id, so a repeated publish within the duplicate window is stored once; a repeated delivery queues nothing new either way.
- The rest works as with Redis: payloads are checked against the subscriber's schema (IL6034), the trace and the tenant travel with the event, and `app.events.transport` is `"nats"`. Invalid arguments raise IL6051.
- Options: `service` (required), `stream` (default `"INFERLO_EVENTS"`, the same in every service), `maxAgeMs` (used when the stream is created), `staleAfterMs`, `batch` (events read per event and poll, default 100). Close the NATS connection after `app.close()`.

### RabbitMQ

Services that already run RabbitMQ use `rabbitmqEventTransport` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/rabbitmq` with a connection from [amqplib](https://amqp-node.github.io/amqplib/) (0.10.9 or later, promise API; RabbitMQ 4.3 or later):

```ts
import amqp from "amqplib";
import { rabbitmqEventTransport } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/rabbitmq";

const connection = await amqp.connect(settings.RABBITMQ_URL);

export const app = createApp({
  name: "billing",
  jobs: [jobs],                        // on(orderPaid, createInvoice)
  events: { transport: rabbitmqEventTransport(connection, { service: "billing" }) },
});
```

- Events are published to the durable topic exchange `inferlo.events` with the event name as routing key, as persistent JSON messages with the event id as `messageId`. Publishing uses publisher confirms: `events.publish(...)` resolves when RabbitMQ has the event, and rejects when it refused it.
- Each service reads each event it subscribes to from its own durable queue, `inferlo.<service>.<event name>`, declared and bound at its first read (a quorum queue, or `queueType: "classic"`). Instances of one service share its queues, so each service gets each event once. Pass the app's name as `service`. A service only gets the events published after its first read.
- An event is acknowledged after its jobs are queued. One whose delivery fails (its jobs could not be queued) is returned to its queue after `staleAfterMs` (default 30000); the events an instance read without acknowledging are returned when its connection closes. A repeated delivery queues nothing new.
- RabbitMQ 4 drops a message from a quorum queue after 20 deliveries by default (about 10 minutes of failed deliveries with the default `staleAfterMs`). To keep events longer while a dependency is down, set a policy for the queues, for example `rabbitmqctl set_policy inferlo-events "^inferlo\." '{"delivery-limit": -1}' --apply-to quorum_queues`, or a `dead-letter-exchange` to keep them aside.
- Messages in the queues that are not Inferlo events are acknowledged and dropped. The rest works as with Redis: payloads are checked against the subscriber's schema (IL6034), the trace and the tenant travel with the event, and `app.events.transport` is `"rabbitmq"`. Invalid arguments raise IL6054.
- Options: `service` (required), `exchange` (default `"inferlo.events"`, the same in every service), `queueType` (`"quorum"` or `"classic"`), `staleAfterMs`, `batch` (events read per event and poll, default 100). Close the connection after `app.close()`.

## Where jobs are kept

By default the queue is kept in memory in the process that enqueues, so jobs are lost on restart and every instance runs its own. That is right for development and tests.

In production, keep jobs in Postgres or Redis. In Postgres:

```ts
export const app = createApp({
  db: postgres({ url: env("DATABASE_URL") }),
  jobs: [jobs],
  jobQueue: { store: "database" },     // default "memory"
});
```

- Jobs are stored in the table `inferlo_jobs`, created on first use (no migration needed). They survive restarts and deploys. With `createApp({ tracing })`, a job also stores the trace it was enqueued in, so its run shows up in the same trace (see [Observability, "Jobs"](observability.md#jobs)).
- Every instance shares the queue. Due jobs are claimed with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so each attempt runs on exactly one instance, however many run `app.jobs.start()`.
- An instance only claims jobs it has registered, so during a rolling deploy an old instance never picks up a job that only the new code knows.
- While a job runs, its worker reports every 30 seconds that it is still alive. A job still `"running"` without a report for 5 minutes (its process crashed or was killed) is picked up again as its next attempt, with `lastError` saying the worker stopped. If it has no attempts left, it is marked `"failed"` instead. This is why handlers must be safe to run twice.
- `{ store: "database" }` needs the Postgres adapter (IL6012). Any other store name raises IL6011.
- `app.jobs.get(id)` reads the record from the table, so any instance can check a job's status.

Or keep them in Redis, with the same guarantees:

```ts
const redis = await createClient({ url: settings.REDIS_URL }).connect();   // from the redis package

export const app = createApp({
  redis,
  jobs: [jobs],
  jobQueue: { store: "redis" },
});
```

- Each due job is claimed by one atomic Lua script, so each attempt runs on exactly one instance. Retries, backoff, the registered-jobs rule, the 30-second reports and the 5-minute stuck-job rule work as with the database queue; whether a job is stuck is decided with the Redis server's clock, so instances whose clocks differ agree.
- Pending and running jobs never expire. Finished jobs (`"done"` or `"failed"`) are kept for 7 days, so `app.jobs.get(id)` can report them, then Redis removes them.
- Cron ticks are queued once across instances, as with the database queue.
- `{ store: "redis" }` without `createApp({ redis })` raises IL6031. Keys and other details are in [Redis](redis.md#job-queue).

### BullMQ

Apps that already run [BullMQ](https://docs.bullmq.io) (5.0.0 or later) can keep Inferlo's jobs in a BullMQ queue, so they show up in the same dashboards (Bull Board, Taskforce.sh) and use the same Redis. Pass a `Queue` and a `Worker` of that queue without a processor to `bullmqJobStore` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/bullmq`:

```ts
import { Queue, Worker } from "bullmq";
import { bullmqJobStore } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/bullmq";

const connection = new IORedis(settings.REDIS_URL, { maxRetriesPerRequest: null });   // from the ioredis package
const queue = new Queue("inferlo", { connection });
const worker = new Worker("inferlo", null, { connection, autorun: false });

export const app = createApp({
  jobs: [jobs],
  jobQueue: { store: bullmqJobStore(queue, worker) },
});
```

- Every Inferlo job is a BullMQ job: its name is the job's name, its id is Inferlo's job id, and `runAt` is BullMQ's delay. Jobs queued with the same id (cron ticks, the jobs of an event delivered twice) are queued once, as with the other stores.
- Inferlo takes jobs with BullMQ's manual processing API in `app.jobs.start()`, `inferlo worker` and `app.jobs.runDue()`, and runs them with its own handlers, so input validation, retries with Inferlo's backoff (`moveToDelayed`), tracing, tenants, metrics and `onError` work as with the other stores. A finished job is `completed` or `failed` in BullMQ, kept for 7 days.
- While a job runs, its lock is extended every `lockDuration / 2` (the worker's option, default 30 seconds). A job whose process stopped is moved back by BullMQ's stalled-job check and runs again as its next attempt, with `lastError` saying the worker stopped, or is failed when it has no attempts left. BullMQ fails a job that stalled more than the worker's `maxStalledCount` times (default 1); raise it for long deploys. Handlers must be safe to run twice.
- Give Inferlo its own queue: a job in it that Inferlo did not queue is failed with a message, and BullMQ hands out jobs in order whatever their name, so a job that an older instance has not registered fails with IL6010 and is retried (deploy every instance with the same jobs). BullMQ decides when a job is due with its own clock, so `runDue({ now })` cannot run jobs early.
- The worker must belong to the same queue and be created with `autorun: false` and no processor, so only Inferlo takes its jobs; other arguments raise IL6057. Close the worker and the queue after `app.close()`.

## Testing

`app.jobs.runDue()` runs every due job now, one after another, including follow-ups they enqueue, and returns `{ done, retried, failed }`:

```ts
const res = await app.request("/notes", { method: "POST", json: { title: "Hi", body: "..." }, as: user });
assert.deepEqual(await app.jobs.runDue(), { done: 1, retried: 0, failed: 0 });
```

`runDue({ now })` runs the jobs that are due at that time, to test retries and `runAt` without waiting.

`inferlo describe` lists jobs with their retries and input schema, crons with their schedule, and events with their payload and subscribed jobs. To test the jobs of an event, publish it with `await app.events.publish(orderPaid, payload)`, then run `await app.jobs.runDue()`.

---

# Caching

Every app has a cache for results that are slow or expensive to compute, and GET routes can cache their whole responses (see [Caching route responses](#caching-route-responses)): reports, counts, responses from other services, AI answers that do not change often. It is `ctx.cache` in routes and jobs and `app.cache` everywhere else (scripts, tests, server startup), all the same cache.

```ts
import { route } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const ticketStats = route.get("/tickets/stats", { summary: "Ticket counts by status" }).handle(({ db, cache }) =>
  cache.getOrSet("tickets:stats", { ttlMs: 60_000, tags: ["tickets"] }, async () => {
    const all = await db.tickets.findMany({});
    return { open: all.filter((t) => t.status === "open").length, total: all.length };
  }),
);

export const closeTicket = route.post("/tickets/:id/close", { params: IdParams }).handle(async ({ db, cache, params }) => {
  const ticket = await db.tickets.update(params.id, { status: "closed" });
  await cache.invalidate("tickets"); // every entry tagged "tickets" is removed
  return ticket;
});
```

## The API

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `await cache.getOrSet(key, { ttlMs, tags }, compute)` | The cached value, or else the result of `compute()`, stored for `ttlMs`. Concurrent calls for the same key in one process share one `compute()` call. When `compute()` throws, nothing is stored and the error is thrown. |
| `await cache.get(key)` | The cached value, or `undefined` when there is none or it expired. `cache.get<Stats>(key)` types the result. |
| `await cache.set(key, value, { ttlMs, tags })` | Store a value for `ttlMs` milliseconds, replacing any entry with the same key. |
| `await cache.delete(key)` | Remove one entry. |
| `await cache.invalidate("tickets")` or `invalidate(["tickets", "users"])` | Remove every entry stored with any of these tags. |
| `await cache.clear()` | Remove every entry. |
| `cache.store` | `"memory"` or `"database"`. |

Prefer `getOrSet`: it is one call, and it cannot forget to store the result.

- **Every entry has a time to live.** `ttlMs` is required, a whole number of milliseconds from 1 to 365 days. There is no entry that lives forever, so stale data always goes away on its own.
- **Tags invalidate groups of entries.** Tag entries with what they depend on (`"tickets"`, `` `user:${user.id}` ``) and call `invalidate` with that tag after a change. This is how to keep cached data correct when the data changes before the time to live is over.
- **Values are stored as JSON.** Plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and `null`. Dates come back as ISO strings, also from `getOrSet` on the first call, so a hit and a miss return the same thing. `undefined`, functions and `BigInt` cannot be cached (IL6028); cache `null` for "nothing". The memory store keeps JSON too, so changing an object you stored or got never changes the cached entry.
- **Keys** are strings of 1 to 512 characters. Build them from what the value depends on: `` `tickets:stats` ``, `` `user:${user.id}:dashboard` ``. A value that differs per user must have the user in its key, so one user never sees another user's data.

## Stores

```ts
createApp({ cache: { store: "memory" } });   // default
createApp({ cache: { store: "database" }, db: postgres({ url: settings.DATABASE_URL }) });
createApp({ cache: { store: "redis" }, redis });   // redis = await createClient({ url }).connect()
```

- `"memory"` (default): entries live in the process. Fast and fine for one instance and for tests, but each instance has its own entries, and `invalidate` only reaches the instance that calls it. It keeps at most `maxEntries` entries (default 10000; `{ store: "memory", maxEntries: 50_000 }`) and removes the least recently used first.
- `"database"`: entries live in the `inferlo_cache` table of the app's Postgres database (created on first use), so every instance shares them and `invalidate` and `delete` reach all of them. Expired entries are never returned and are removed from time to time. Apps that share one database share this table, so give their keys and tags a prefix. It needs `postgres()` as the database; with another adapter `createApp` raises IL6028.

- `"redis"`: entries live in the Redis of `createApp({ redis })` (see [Redis](redis.md)), so every instance shares them and `invalidate`, `delete` and `clear` reach all of them. Redis expires entries itself. Keys start with `inferlo:<app name>:cache:`, so apps that share one Redis keep their entries apart, and `clear()` removes only the app's own. Without `createApp({ redis })` it raises IL6031.

`inferlo describe` and `app.describe().cache` show which store an app uses.

## Caching route responses

A GET route can cache its whole JSON response with the `cache` option, without changing the handler:

```ts
export const ticketStats = route
  .get("/tickets/stats", { cache: { ttlMs: 60_000, tags: ["tickets"] } })
  .handle(async ({ db, user }) => ({ open: await db.tickets.count({ ownerId: user.id, status: "open" }) }));
```

| Option | |
|---|---|
| `ttlMs` | Required. How long a response is kept, in milliseconds (1 to 365 days). |
| `by` | `"user"` (default): each signed-in user gets their own cached response (requests without a user share one). `"tenant"`: the users of one tenant (organisation) in [multi-tenant apps](database.md#multi-tenancy) share a cached response, and users without a tenant get their own. `"public"`: every caller gets the same response; use it only when the response does not depend on the user. |
| `tags` | Tags for `ctx.cache.invalidate(tag)`, so a change removes the cached responses at once. |

- **Checks still run.** Auth, roles, `permission`, `rateLimit` and the `query` and `params` schemas run on every request before the cache is read, so a cached response only reaches callers who may call the route with valid input. Only the handler is skipped.
- **One entry per URL.** The key is the route, who shares it (`by`) and the full path and query string (in any parameter order), so `/tickets?page=2` and `/tickets?page=3` are cached separately.
- **What is cached.** Answers with status 200 that the handler returned as a value (JSON), with the headers the handler set itself (`header(name, value)`). A handler that returns a `Response` (streams, files), another status, `undefined` (204), or sets a cookie is never cached. Per-request headers (request id, rate limit, CORS) are always fresh.
- **Headers.** Every response of a cached route has `X-Inferlo-Cache: HIT` or `MISS` and an `ETag`; a request with a matching `If-None-Match` gets `304 Not Modified` without a body. `Cache-Control` is `private, no-cache` (or `public, no-cache` for `by: "public"` on an `auth: "public"` route), so browsers and CDNs revalidate instead of serving a copy that `invalidate` cannot reach; `by: "user"` adds `Vary: Authorization, Cookie`. A `Cache-Control` the handler sets itself is kept.
- **Invalidation.** Call `await cache.invalidate("tickets")` in the routes and jobs that change tickets, as above. Without tags, a cached response is only replaced after `ttlMs`.
- Only GET routes (and their HEAD requests) can be cached; anything else raises IL6028 when the app starts. `describe()`, `inferlo describe` and OpenAPI (`x-inferlo-cache`) show each route's cache.

## In jobs and tests

```ts
export const refreshStats = job("refresh-stats", { input: t.object({}) }).handle(async ({ cache }) => {
  await cache.invalidate("tickets");
});
```

In tests, `app.cache` is the same cache the routes use: check what a route stored with `await app.cache.get(key)`, or start from a clean cache with `await app.cache.clear()`.

---

# File storage

`ctx.storage` keeps files, such as uploads from [`t.file()`](routes.md#file-uploads), in the store chosen in `createApp({ storage })`. It works the same in routes, WebSocket handlers and jobs, and as `app.storage` everywhere else.

```ts
import { createApp, diskStorage, env, route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const uploadAvatar = route
  .post("/me/avatar", { body: t.object({ avatar: t.file({ maxBytes: 2_000_000, types: ["image/png", "image/jpeg"] }) }) })
  .handle(async ({ body, user, storage, db }) => {
    const saved = await storage.put(`avatars/${user.id}`, body.avatar); // { key, size, type }
    await db.users.update(user.id, { avatarKey: saved.key });
    return saved;
  });

export const app = createApp({
  routes,
  storage: diskStorage({ dir: env("UPLOADS_DIR", { default: "./uploads" }) }),
});
```

## Stores

| Store | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `memoryStorage()` | Tests and single-process development. Files are lost on restart. |
| `diskStorage({ dir })` | A local disk, or a volume every instance mounts (NFS, EFS, a Kubernetes persistent volume). Node.js, Bun and Deno. The directory is created on first write. |
| `s3Storage({ bucket, region, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey })` | An S3-compatible object store shared by every instance: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO and others. Needs only `fetch` and Web Crypto. Gives [signed download URLs](#signed-download-urls). See [S3, R2 and MinIO](#s3-r2-and-minio). |
| Your own `StorageStore` | Any other store: an object with `name`, `put(key, bytes, type)`, `get(key)` (resolves to `{ bytes, type }` or `null`) and `delete(key)` (resolves to `true` when the key existed), and optionally `url(key, expiresIn)` for signed URLs. |

Without a `storage` option, `ctx.storage` throws IL6037 (a 500 in routes), so files are never kept somewhere you did not choose. An invalid option fails at startup with IL6038.

## The API

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `await storage.put(key, data, { type })` | Stores `data` (a `File` from `t.file()`, a `Blob`, a `Uint8Array`, an `ArrayBuffer` or a string) under `key`, replacing what was there. Resolves to `{ key, size, type }`. |
| `await storage.get(key)` | The file as a web `File` (`name` is the key's last segment, `type` the stored media type), or `null`. |
| `await storage.delete(key)` | Removes the file. Resolves to `true` when it existed, `false` otherwise. |
| `await storage.url(key, { expiresIn })` | A signed URL that downloads the file without credentials for `expiresIn` seconds (1 to 604800, seven days). Only stores that sign URLs have it (`s3Storage`); memory and disk stores throw IL6050. See [Signed download URLs](#signed-download-urls). |
| `storage.store` | The store's name (`"memory"`, `"disk"`, `"s3"` or your store's `name`), or `null` without a storage option. `inferlo describe` shows it as `storage`. |

- The media type is `{ type }` when given, else the `File`'s or `Blob`'s type without parameters, else `application/octet-stream`. It must be a plain media type such as `image/png` (lower-cased when stored); anything else is IL6039.
- Keys are segments of letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, separated by `/`, up to 1024 characters: `avatars/42.png`, `tenants/acme/reports/2026-11.pdf`. A segment cannot start with `.` and cannot be empty, so `..`, `/etc/passwd`, `a//b` and hidden files are refused with IL6039 before any store sees them.
- Never use a file name sent by the client as the key. Build keys from ids you control, and keep the key in a `t.string()` field of a model.
- Keys are the same for every user and tenant. In a [multi-tenant app](database.md#multi-tenancy), put the tenant in the key (`` `tenants/${user.tenantId}/...` ``) and check access in the route before reading a file.

## Serving files

Return a `Response` with the file. Send it as an attachment unless you know the type is safe to show, because an HTML or SVG file shown inline runs in your site's origin:

```ts
import { notFound, route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const downloadReport = route.get("/reports/:id", { params: t.object({ id: t.uuid() }) }).handle(async ({ params, storage, db, user }) => {
  const report = await db.reports.findOne({ where: { id: params.id, ownerId: user.id } });
  if (!report) throw notFound("Report not found.");
  const file = await storage.get(report.fileKey);
  if (!file) throw notFound("Report file not found.");
  return new Response(file, {
    headers: { "content-type": file.type, "content-disposition": `attachment; filename="${report.id}.pdf"` },
  });
});
```

## S3, R2 and MinIO

`s3Storage()` keeps files in a bucket of any store that speaks the S3 API. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 on Web Crypto and sent with `fetch`, so there is no AWS SDK and no runtime dependency.

```ts
import { createApp, env, s3Storage } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";

export const app = createApp({
  routes,
  storage: s3Storage({
    bucket: env("S3_BUCKET"),
    region: env("S3_REGION"),
    accessKeyId: env("S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID"),
    secretAccessKey: env("S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"),
  }),
});
```

| Store | Options |
|---|---|
| AWS S3 | `bucket`, `region` (`"eu-central-1"`), the access key; leave `endpoint` out. The bucket is addressed by host name (`https://<bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com`). With temporary credentials (an IAM role, AWS STS), also pass `sessionToken`. |
| Cloudflare R2 | `endpoint: "https://<account id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com"`, `region: "auto"`, and an R2 API token's access key id and secret. |
| MinIO and other S3-compatible stores | `endpoint` (`"https://minio.internal.example.com"`, or `"http://localhost:9000"` in development), the region the server is configured with (MinIO's default is `"us-east-1"`), and an access key. |

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bucket` | The bucket name: 3 to 63 lowercase letters, digits, `.` and `-`. The bucket must exist; Inferlo does not create it. |
| `region` | The bucket's region, `"auto"` on R2. |
| `accessKeyId`, `secretAccessKey` | A key that may read, write and delete objects in the bucket (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject`). Read them with `env()`; the secret is never logged, put in an error or in a URL. |
| `sessionToken` | Session token of temporary credentials. |
| `endpoint` | The store's origin for anything but AWS S3. https is required except on `localhost`. No path: the bucket goes in `bucket`. |
| `pathStyle` | `true` addresses the bucket in the path (`https://endpoint/bucket/key`). Default: `true` with an `endpoint`, `false` on AWS S3. Bucket names with dots need it on AWS S3. |
| `timeoutMs` | Time limit of each request to the store, 1000 to 300000 ms (default 30000). |

- Keys are object keys in the bucket as they are: `avatars/42.png` is `s3://<bucket>/avatars/42.png`. To share a bucket between apps, start the keys with the app's name.
- `storage.delete(key)` asks the store whether the key exists before deleting it, because S3 answers a delete the same either way.
- When the store refuses a request or cannot be reached, the call throws IL6049 (a 502 in routes) naming the operation, key, bucket and S3's error code (`AccessDenied`, `NoSuchBucket`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch`), never a credential. A missing key is `null`, but a missing bucket is IL6049.
- Invalid options (an http endpoint that is not localhost, an endpoint with a path, an unknown option) fail at startup with IL6048.
- Each file is sent and read in one request, which suits files up to a few hundred megabytes; keep the `t.file({ maxBytes })` limit of the route below that.

## Signed download URLs

`storage.url(key, { expiresIn })` returns a URL that downloads the file straight from the store, without credentials, for `expiresIn` seconds. Use it for large files, so they do not pass through your app: check access in the route, then redirect.

```ts
export const downloadReport = route.get("/reports/:id", { params: t.object({ id: t.uuid() }) }).handle(async ({ params, storage, db, user }) => {
  const report = await db.reports.findOne({ where: { id: params.id, ownerId: user.id } });
  if (!report) throw notFound("Report not found.");
  return Response.redirect(await storage.url(report.fileKey, { expiresIn: 300 }), 303);
});
```

- `expiresIn` is required, a whole number of seconds from 1 to 604800 (seven days, the S3 limit); anything else is IL6039. Keep it short: anyone who has the URL can download the file until it expires, and it cannot be revoked earlier except by deleting the file or the key that signed it.
- The URL allows `GET` of that one key only.
- The browser receives the file with the media type it was stored with. An HTML or SVG file opened from a signed URL runs in the store's origin, not yours, but still check what you let users upload.
- Stores without signed URLs (`memoryStorage()`, `diskStorage()`) throw IL6050: serve those files from a route as shown in [Serving files](#serving-files).

## How diskStorage writes

Each `put` writes to a temporary file in `dir/.inferlo-tmp/` and renames it into `dir/<key>`, so readers see the old file or the new one, never half of one, and concurrent writes to one key leave one whole file. The media type is kept in `dir/.inferlo-meta/<key>`; files copied into the directory by hand are read as `application/octet-stream`. Keys cannot reach either directory.

For several instances, mount the same volume at `dir` on each, or use [`s3Storage()`](#s3-r2-and-minio).

## Testing

Use `memoryStorage()` and read files back through `app.storage`:

```ts
const app = createApp({ routes, storage: memoryStorage() });
const form = new FormData();
form.append("avatar", new Blob([png], { type: "image/png" }), "me.png");
await app.request("/me/avatar", { method: "POST", body: form, as: user });
assert.equal((await app.storage.get(`avatars/${user.id}`))?.type, "image/png");
```

---

# Redis

Apps with more than one instance need state that every instance sees. Postgres covers this with `store: "database"`; Redis is the other choice, for apps that already run it or want counters off the database. Inferlo has no dependency on a Redis package: you create and connect the client, and Inferlo uses it.

```ts
// src/app.ts
import { createClient } from "redis";
import { createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { settings } from "./settings.ts";

const redis = await createClient({ url: settings.REDIS_URL }).connect();

export const app = createApp({
  name: "boards",
  // ...
  redis,
  rateLimit: { store: "redis" },   // route rateLimit counts, shared by every instance
  cache: { store: "redis" },       // ctx.cache, app.cache and cached routes
  jobQueue: { store: "redis" },    // background jobs and cron ticks
  events: { transport: "redis" },  // events to and from other services (Redis Streams)
  // WebSocket broadcasts to every instance (Redis Pub/Sub, on a second connection)
  sockets: { transport: "redis", subscriber: await redis.duplicate().connect() },
  health: true,                    // GET /ready also checks that Redis answers
});
```

- `redis` is a connected client from the official [`redis`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/redis) package (node-redis 5 or newer). Inferlo talks to it through `client.sendCommand([...])` only, with one key per command. Anything without `sendCommand` raises IL6031. A single Redis server (or a managed endpoint such as Azure Cache, ElastiCache or Upstash with a Redis URL) is supported; Redis Cluster clients (`createCluster`) are not yet.
- ioredis has no `sendCommand` with this shape; wrap it: `redis: { sendCommand: (args) => ioredis.call(args[0]!, ...args.slice(1)) }`.
- Inferlo never connects, reconnects or closes the client. Close it after the app: `await app.close(); await redis.close();`.
- Keys start with `inferlo:<app name>:` (the `name` from `createApp`), so apps that share one Redis keep their keys apart. Give each app its own `name`.

## Rate limits

`createApp({ redis, rateLimit: { store: "redis" } })` keeps the counts of every route's `rateLimit` (see [Rate limiting](routes.md#rate-limiting)) in Redis, one key per route, client and window. Each hit is one atomic Lua script (`INCR`, then `PEXPIRE` on the first hit of a window), so concurrent requests on different instances never over- or under-count, and Redis removes a window's key when it ends. `store: "redis"` without `createApp({ redis })` raises IL6031.

## Cache

`createApp({ redis, cache: { store: "redis" } })` keeps `ctx.cache`, `app.cache` and cached route responses (see [Caching](caching.md)) in Redis:

- Each entry is one key (`inferlo:<app name>:cache:entry:<key>`) with the entry's `ttlMs` as its Redis expiry, so Redis removes expired entries itself.
- Each tag is a Redis set of the entries stored with it. `cache.invalidate(tag)` deletes those entries and the set in one atomic script, on every instance at once. A tag set expires with its longest-lived entry.
- `cache.clear()` walks the app's cache keys with `SCAN` (it does not block Redis like `KEYS`) and deletes them, leaving other apps' keys alone.
