| `HTTPException` | `httpError(status, message)`, `notFound()`, `forbidden()`, `badRequest()` ([errors](routes.md#errors)) |
| `hono/bearer-auth`, `hono/jwt`, `hono/basic-auth` | `createApp({ auth })` with `bearer(...)` or `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }`, and the route's `auth` option ([auth](auth.md)) |
| `hono/cors` | `createApp({ cors: { origin: [...] } })` |
| `hono/secure-headers` | Built in: security headers on every response ([security](security.md)) |
| `hono/logger`, `hono/request-id` | `createApp({ logging: { requests: true } })` and `X-Request-Id` ([observability](observability.md)) |
| `hono/timeout` | `createApp({ requestTimeoutMs })` and the route's `timeoutMs` ([security](security.md#request-timeouts)) |
| `hono.route("/books", books)` sub-apps | Route files, grouped into [modules](modules.md) for larger features |
| `basePath("/v1")` | `apiVersion("v1", routes)`, with an OpenAPI document per version ([API versions](routes.md#api-versions)) |
| `@hono/zod-openapi`, `@hono/swagger-ui` | Generated: `GET /openapi.json` from the route schemas |
| Hono RPC (`hc<AppType>`) | The OpenAPI document for client generators; MCP tools for AI agents |
| `hono/streaming` (`streamSSE`) | `return ctx.ai.stream(...).toResponse()` for model output, or a `Response` with a `ReadableStream` |
| `c.env` bindings and `process.env` | `config({ schema })` in `src/config.ts` ([configuration](config.md)) |
| `app.request()` in tests | `app.request(path, { method, json, as: user })` with a signed-in test user ([testing](testing.md)) |
| `export default hono` | `export default app` (Bun, Deno, Workers) or `app.listen()` on Node.js ([deployment](deploy.md)) |

## 4. Share auth between both

During the migration, Hono and Inferlo routes must accept the same credentials. Put the check in one function and use it from both:

```ts
// src/auth-check.ts
export async function userFromToken(token: string | undefined) {
  if (!token) return null;
  const session = await sessions.findByToken(token); // your existing lookup
  return session ? { id: session.userId, roles: session.roles } : null;
}
```

```ts
// Hono middleware, as before
export const requireUser = createMiddleware(async (c, next) => {
  const user = await userFromToken(c.req.header("authorization")?.replace(/^Bearer /, ""));
  if (!user) return c.json({ error: "Sign in required" }, 401);
  c.set("user", user);
  await next();
});
```

```ts
// src/inferlo/auth.ts
import { bearer } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { userFromToken } from "../auth-check.ts";

export const auth = bearer((token) => userFromToken(token));
```

A user needs an `id`, and `roles` for role-based routes. For cookies or other schemes, write `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }`; `req` is the same standard `Request` Hono gives you as `c.req.raw`.

## 5. Keep your data layer, then adopt models where they fit

Inferlo handlers can call any database code you already have (Drizzle, Prisma, Kysely, a D1 or Postgres client): import it and use it in the handler. You do not have to move data access to switch routes.

For new tables, use Inferlo [models](database.md): validated inserts and updates, typed queries, relations, pagination and generated migrations (`inferlo db migrate`). Inferlo models expect a `uuid` `id`, `created_at` and `updated_at` columns and snake_case column names, so existing tables that differ are best left with your current code.

## 6. Move the tests

```ts
// Before: Hono's app.request with a token
const res = await hono.request("/tickets", { method: "POST", headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "content-type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Printer" }) });

// After: signed in as a test user, JSON body without headers
import { readJson } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/testing";

const res = await app.request("/tickets", { method: "POST", json: { title: "Printer" }, as: { id: "u1", roles: [] } });
const ticket = await readJson(res, 201);
```

Tests through the Hono app (`hono.request(...)`) keep working during the migration, because the catch-all passes requests on to Inferlo.

## 7. Remove Hono

When the last Hono route is gone, export the Inferlo app instead:

```ts
// src/index.ts on Bun, Deno or Cloudflare Workers
import { app } from "./inferlo/app.ts";
export default app;
```

```ts
// src/server.ts on Node.js
import { app } from "./inferlo/app.ts";

const server = await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${server.port}`);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close({ delayMs: 5000 }));
```

Then remove `hono`, its validator and OpenAPI packages and the middleware Inferlo replaced. Compare your app with a new project from `npx @browserlessapi/inferlo new` for the recommended layout, configuration and AGENTS.md for AI coding tools.

## Checklist

- [ ] `hono.all("*", (c) => inferlo.fetch(c.req.raw))` after every Hono route
- [ ] One auth check shared by Hono and Inferlo
- [ ] Each moved route: schemas for its input, the right `auth`, `status(201)` where clients expect it, the Hono route deleted, a test with `app.request`
- [ ] Hono's CORS and security header middleware scoped to Hono routes (Inferlo sends its own)
- [ ] Clients told about the new error format, if they read error bodies
- [ ] Hono removed, `export default app` (or `app.listen()` and `app.close()` on Node.js)

If you only want Inferlo's AI features inside Hono and no migration, use `c.var.ai` from [`@browserlessapi/inferlo/hono`](integrations.md#hono) instead.

---

# Migrate from Koa

This guide moves an existing Koa app (Koa 2 or 3) to Inferlo one route at a time. The app keeps running in the same Node.js process and keeps its URLs during the whole migration: Inferlo answers the routes you have moved, Koa answers the rest. Nothing has to be rewritten in one go.

What you gain on every route you move: validation and types from one schema instead of hand-written checks, routes private by default, the same error format everywhere (`ILxxxx` codes), a database layer with migrations, rate limits, background jobs, an OpenAPI document and an MCP server generated from the routes, and AI models through `ctx.ai`. See [comparison](comparison.md) for the bigger picture.

## 1. Add Inferlo next to Koa

```bash
npm install @browserlessapi/inferlo
```

Create an empty Inferlo app beside your Koa code, for example in `src/inferlo/app.ts`:

```ts
// src/inferlo/app.ts
import { createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { auth } from "./auth.ts";
import * as tickets from "./routes/tickets.ts";

export const app = createApp({
  name: "helpdesk",
  routes: [tickets],
  auth,
  logging: { requests: true },
});
```

Mount it with `toKoaMiddleware(app, { fallthrough: true })` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/koa`, **before** your Koa router:

```ts
// src/server.ts (your existing Koa entry point)
import Koa from "koa";
import Router from "@koa/router";
import bodyParser from "@koa/bodyparser";
import { toKoaMiddleware } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/koa";
import { app as inferlo } from "./inferlo/app.ts";

const koa = new Koa();
const router = new Router();

router.get("/users/:id", requireUser, getUser);   // not moved yet: Koa answers

koa.use(bodyParser());
koa.use(toKoaMiddleware(inferlo, { fallthrough: true })); // Inferlo's routes, OpenAPI and MCP; everything else goes on
koa.use(router.routes()).use(router.allowedMethods());

koa.listen(3000);
```

With `fallthrough: true`, Inferlo answers only the requests it has a route for (method and path) and its own endpoints (`/openapi.json`, `/mcp`, health, metrics and CORS preflights of its paths), and calls `next()` for everything else, so Koa's router keeps answering what it had, including other methods on the same path. As you move routes, more requests stop at Inferlo; nothing else changes.

- Body parsers: when `@koa/bodyparser` or `koa-bodyparser` runs first, Inferlo uses `ctx.request.body`; when Inferlo comes first, it reads the request itself. Either order works.
- Middleware added before Inferlo (logging, request ids) also runs for its requests. Inferlo answers moved routes itself, so Koa middleware after it (and code that runs after `await next()` and sets `ctx.body`) does not touch Inferlo's responses.
- To keep the new routes under their own path for a while, use a prefix instead: `koa.use(toKoaMiddleware(inferlo, { prefix: "/v2" }))` serves the app under `/v2` and passes other paths on. To use only Inferlo's AI features in Koa middleware, see [`inferloAI()`](integrations.md#koa).

## 2. Move one route

Before, in Koa with `@koa/router` and a hand-written check:

```ts
router.post("/tickets", requireUser, async (ctx) => {
  const { title, priority = "normal" } = ctx.request.body ?? {};
  if (typeof title !== "string" || title.length < 3 || title.length > 200) ctx.throw(422, "title must be 3 to 200 characters");
  if (!["low", "normal", "urgent"].includes(priority)) ctx.throw(422, "invalid priority");
  const ticket = await tickets.insert({ title, priority, ownerId: ctx.state.user.id });
  ctx.status = 201;
  ctx.body = ticket;
});
```

After, in Inferlo:

```ts
// src/inferlo/routes/tickets.ts
import { route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { tickets } from "../../db.ts"; // your existing data access code

export const createTicket = route
  .post("/tickets", {
    body: t.object({
      title: t.string().min(3).max(200),
      priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]).default("normal"),
    }),
    summary: "Create a ticket",
  })
  .handle(async ({ body, user, status }) => {
    status(201);
    return tickets.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id });
  });
```

Then delete the Koa route. Requests to `POST /tickets` now stop at Inferlo, at the same URL.

- The schema replaces the hand-written checks (or `koa-joi-router`, `koa-zod-router` and similar): invalid input gets `422` with IL1001 and every problem listed, and `body` is typed. `query` and `params` schemas convert and check `ctx.query` and `ctx.params`.
- The route is private by default: `user` is the signed-in user (no more `ctx.state.user`), and requests without one get `401` (IL3001). This replaces `requireUser`, `koa-jwt` or `koa-passport` checks. Add `auth: "public"` to routes anyone may call, or a role name such as `auth: "admin"`.
- Return the value instead of setting `ctx.body`; call `status(201)` instead of `ctx.status = 201`. `undefined` sends `204`. Return a `Response` for anything that is not JSON.
- Throw `notFound()`, `forbidden()` or `httpError(409, "...")` instead of `ctx.throw(...)` or `http-errors`.
- The error format changes to Inferlo's `{ "error": { "code", "message", ... } }`. If clients parse error bodies, tell them, or move routes in groups that one client uses.

## 3. Map Koa concepts to Inferlo

| Koa | Inferlo |
|---|---|
| `router.get(path, ...middleware, handler)` (`@koa/router`) | `export const x = route.get(path, options).handle(handler)` in a routes file, registered with `createApp({ routes: [file] })` |
| `ctx.params`, `ctx.query`, `ctx.request.body` | `params`, `query`, `body` in the handler context, validated by schemas ([schemas](schema.md)) |
| `ctx.body = value`, `ctx.status = 201` | `return value` and `status(201)` |
| `ctx.set(name, value)` | `header(name, value)` |
| `ctx.state` | `state` from `createApp({ middleware })`, and `user` from auth |
| `ctx.throw(404)`, `http-errors` | `notFound()`, `forbidden()`, `badRequest()`, `httpError(status, message)` ([errors](routes.md#errors)) |
| Error-handling middleware (`try { await next() } catch`) | Built in: every error becomes the standard error body, and unexpected errors are logged with secrets redacted |
| `koa-compose`, middleware chains per route | `createApp({ middleware })` for cross-cutting code, the route's `auth`, `permission` and `rateLimit` options for checks |
| `koa-jwt`, `koa-passport`, custom auth middleware | `createApp({ auth })` with `bearer(...)` or `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }`, and the route's `auth` option ([auth](auth.md)) |
| `koa-bodyparser`, `@koa/bodyparser`, `@koa/multer` | Built in for JSON and forms, with `createApp({ maxBodySize })` |
| `@koa/cors` | `createApp({ cors: { origin: [...] } })` |
| `koa-helmet` | Built in: security headers on every response ([security](security.md)) |
| `koa-ratelimit` | The route's `rateLimit: { max, per, by }`, with memory or Postgres stores ([routes](routes.md)) |
| `koa-logger`, request id middleware | `createApp({ logging: { requests: true } })` and `X-Request-Id` ([observability](observability.md)) |
| `koa-mount`, nested routers with a prefix | Route files, grouped into [modules](modules.md); `apiVersion("v1", routes)` for `/v1` ([API versions](routes.md#api-versions)) |
| `koa-swagger-decorator`, `koa2-swagger-ui` | Generated: `GET /openapi.json` from the route schemas |
| `ctx.req` streaming, server-sent events | `return ctx.ai.stream(...).toResponse()` for model output, or a `Response` with a `ReadableStream` |
| `dotenv`, `process.env` | `config({ schema })` in `src/config.ts` ([configuration](config.md)) |
| `supertest(koa.callback())` in tests | `app.request(path, { method, json, as: user })` with a signed-in test user ([testing](testing.md)) |
| `koa.listen(3000)` | `app.listen(3000)` and `app.close()` on SIGTERM ([deployment](deploy.md)) |

`koa-static`, `koa-views` and `koa-session` have no Inferlo equivalent yet: keep them in Koa (they are not routes you need to move), or serve static files from a CDN or reverse proxy.

## 4. Share auth between both

During the migration, Koa and Inferlo routes must accept the same credentials. Put the check in one function and use it from both:

```ts
// src/auth-check.ts
export async function userFromToken(token: string | undefined) {
  if (!token) return null;
  const session = await sessions.findByToken(token); // your existing lookup
  return session ? { id: session.userId, roles: session.roles } : null;
}
```

```ts
// Koa middleware, as before
export const requireUser: Koa.Middleware = async (ctx, next) => {
  const user = await userFromToken(ctx.get("authorization").replace(/^Bearer /, "") || undefined);
  if (!user) ctx.throw(401, "Sign in required");
  ctx.state.user = user;
  await next();
};
```

```ts
// src/inferlo/auth.ts
import { bearer } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { userFromToken } from "../auth-check.ts";

export const auth = bearer((token) => userFromToken(token));
```

A user needs an `id`, and `roles` for role-based routes. For cookie sessions or other schemes, write `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }`; `req` is a standard `Request` with the same headers and cookies Koa sees.

## 5. Keep your data layer, then adopt models where they fit

Inferlo handlers can call any database code you already have (Knex, Sequelize, TypeORM, Prisma, Drizzle, a `pg` pool): import it and use it in the handler. You do not have to move data access to switch routes. For writes across your existing tables and new Inferlo models in one transaction, see [Drizzle](integrations.md#drizzle-orm), [Kysely](integrations.md#kysely), [Knex](integrations.md#knex), [Prisma](integrations.md#prisma), [TypeORM](integrations.md#typeorm) and [Sequelize](integrations.md#sequelize).

For new tables, use Inferlo [models](database.md): validated inserts and updates, typed queries, relations, pagination and generated migrations (`inferlo db migrate`). Inferlo models expect a `uuid` `id`, `created_at` and `updated_at` columns and snake_case column names, so existing tables that differ are best left with your current code.

## 6. Move the tests

```ts
// Before: supertest with a token
const res = await request(koa.callback()).post("/tickets").set("authorization", `Bearer ${token}`).send({ title: "Printer" });

// After: signed in as a test user, without a server
import { readJson } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/testing";

const res = await app.request("/tickets", { method: "POST", json: { title: "Printer" }, as: { id: "u1", roles: [] } });
const ticket = await readJson(res, 201);
```

Supertest tests against `koa.callback()` keep working during the migration, because moved routes are answered at the same URLs.

## 7. Remove Koa

When the last Koa route is gone, start the Inferlo app directly:

```ts
// src/server.ts
import { app } from "./inferlo/app.ts";

const server = await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${server.port}`);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close({ delayMs: 5000 }));
```

Then remove `koa`, `@koa/router`, the body parser and the middleware Inferlo replaced. Compare your app with a new project from `npx @browserlessapi/inferlo new` for the recommended layout, configuration and AGENTS.md for AI coding tools.

## Checklist

- [ ] `koa.use(toKoaMiddleware(inferlo, { fallthrough: true }))` before the Koa router
- [ ] One auth check shared by Koa and Inferlo
- [ ] Each moved route: schemas for its input, the right `auth`, `status(201)` where clients expect it, the Koa route deleted, a test with `app.request`
- [ ] Koa's CORS and helmet middleware scoped to Koa routes (Inferlo sends its own headers)
- [ ] Clients told about the new error format, if they read error bodies
- [ ] Koa removed, `app.listen()` and `app.close()` on SIGTERM

If you only want Inferlo's AI features inside Koa and no migration, use `ctx.ai` from [`@browserlessapi/inferlo/koa`](integrations.md#koa) instead.

---

# Migrate from Fastify

This guide moves an existing Fastify app (Fastify 5) to Inferlo one route at a time. The app keeps running in the same Node.js process and keeps its URLs during the whole migration: Inferlo answers the routes you have moved, Fastify answers the rest. Nothing has to be rewritten in one go.

What you gain on every route you move: validation and types from one schema instead of JSON schemas plus separate TypeScript types, routes private by default, the same error format everywhere (`ILxxxx` codes), a database layer with migrations, rate limits, background jobs, an OpenAPI document and an MCP server generated from the routes, and AI models through `ctx.ai`. See [comparison](comparison.md) for the bigger picture.

## 1. Add Inferlo next to Fastify

```bash
npm install @browserlessapi/inferlo
```

Create an empty Inferlo app beside your Fastify code, for example in `src/inferlo/app.ts`:

```ts
// src/inferlo/app.ts
import { createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { auth } from "./auth.ts";
import * as tickets from "./routes/tickets.ts";

export const app = createApp({
  name: "helpdesk",
  routes: [tickets],
  auth,
  logging: { requests: true },
});
```

Register it with `inferloPlugin` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/fastify` and `fallthrough: true`:

```ts
// src/server.ts (your existing Fastify entry point)
import Fastify from "fastify";
import { inferloPlugin } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/fastify";
import { app as inferlo } from "./inferlo/app.ts";

const fastify = Fastify({ logger: true });

await fastify.register(cors, { origin: ["https://app.example.com"] });
fastify.get("/users/:id", { preHandler: requireUser }, getUser);   // not moved yet: Fastify answers

await fastify.register(inferloPlugin, { app: inferlo, fallthrough: true }); // Inferlo's routes, OpenAPI and MCP

await fastify.listen({ port: 3000 });
```

With `fallthrough: true`, Inferlo answers only the requests it has a route for (method and path) and its own endpoints (`/openapi.json`, `/mcp`, health, metrics and CORS preflights of its paths), in an `onRequest` hook, before Fastify reads the body. Every other request goes on to Fastify's router as before, including other methods on the same path and Fastify's own 404 handler. As you move routes, more requests stop at Inferlo; nothing else changes.

- Order: where you register the plugin does not change which requests Inferlo answers. `onRequest` hooks added before it on the root instance (request ids, logging) also run for Inferlo's requests; hooks added after it, hooks inside encapsulated plugins and the later hooks (`preParsing`, `preValidation`, `preHandler`, `onSend`) do not, because Inferlo answers the request itself.
- Body parsing: Inferlo reads the request body itself (JSON, forms, its own `maxBodySize`), so Fastify's content type parsers and `bodyLimit` stay as they are for your Fastify routes.
- Global plugins that change responses (`@fastify/cors`, `@fastify/helmet`, `@fastify/compress`) work through `onSend` and similar hooks, so they do not apply to Inferlo's responses. Inferlo sends its own CORS and security headers; configure them in `createApp`.
- To keep the new routes under their own path for a while, add a prefix: `{ app: inferlo, prefix: "/v2", fallthrough: true }` answers the app's routes under `/v2` only. Without `fallthrough`, `{ app, prefix: "/v2" }` gives the whole prefix to Inferlo, including its 404s. To use only Inferlo's AI features in Fastify routes, see [`fastify.ai` and `request.ai`](integrations.md#fastify-1).

## 2. Move one route

Before, in Fastify with a JSON schema, a TypeScript type for the same body and an auth hook:

```ts
interface CreateTicket { title: string; priority?: "low" | "normal" | "urgent" }

fastify.post<{ Body: CreateTicket }>(
  "/tickets",
  {
    preHandler: requireUser,
    schema: {
      body: {
        type: "object",
        required: ["title"],
        properties: {
          title: { type: "string", minLength: 3, maxLength: 200 },
          priority: { type: "string", enum: ["low", "normal", "urgent"], default: "normal" },
        },
      },
    },
  },
  async (request, reply) => {
    const ticket = await tickets.insert({ ...request.body, ownerId: request.user.id });
    return reply.code(201).send(ticket);
  },
);
```

After, in Inferlo:

```ts
// src/inferlo/routes/tickets.ts
import { route, t } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { tickets } from "../../db.ts"; // your existing data access code

export const createTicket = route
  .post("/tickets", {
    body: t.object({
      title: t.string().min(3).max(200),
      priority: t.enum(["low", "normal", "urgent"]).default("normal"),
    }),
    summary: "Create a ticket",
  })
  .handle(async ({ body, user, status }) => {
    status(201);
    return tickets.insert({ ...body, ownerId: user.id });
  });
```

Then delete the Fastify route. Requests to `POST /tickets` now stop at Inferlo, at the same URL.

- One `t.*` schema replaces the JSON schema and the TypeScript type (or a TypeBox or Zod type provider): invalid input gets `422` with IL1001 and every problem listed, and `body` is typed. `query` and `params` schemas replace `schema.querystring` and `schema.params` and convert strings to numbers and booleans the same way. `response` replaces `schema.response` for the OpenAPI document.
- The route is private by default: `user` is the signed-in user (no more `request.user` from a decorator), and requests without one get `401` (IL3001). This replaces `preHandler: requireUser`, `@fastify/jwt` with `request.jwtVerify()` and `@fastify/auth`. Add `auth: "public"` to routes anyone may call, or a role name such as `auth: "admin"`.
- Return the value; call `status(201)` instead of `reply.code(201)` and `header(name, value)` instead of `reply.header(...)`. `undefined` sends `204`. Return a `Response` for anything that is not JSON.
- Throw `notFound()`, `forbidden()` or `httpError(409, "...")` instead of `reply.code(404).send(...)` or `@fastify/sensible`'s `reply.notFound()` and `fastify.httpErrors`.
- The error format changes from Fastify's `{ statusCode, error, message }` to Inferlo's `{ "error": { "code", "message", ... } }`. If clients parse error bodies, tell them, or move routes in groups that one client uses.

## 3. Map Fastify concepts to Inferlo

| Fastify | Inferlo |
|---|---|
| `fastify.get(path, options, handler)`, route shorthand and `fastify.route({ ... })` | `export const x = route.get(path, options).handle(handler)` in a routes file, registered with `createApp({ routes: [file] })` |
| `schema: { body, querystring, params }` (Ajv JSON schemas), type providers | `body`, `query` and `params` with `t.*` schemas: validation and types from one definition ([schemas](schema.md)) |
| `schema.response` and fast-json-stringify | `response: schema` on the route, used for OpenAPI |
| `request.body`, `request.query`, `request.params` | `body`, `query`, `params` in the handler context |
| `return value`, `reply.code(201)`, `reply.header()` | `return value`, `status(201)`, `header(name, value)` |
| Plugins with `fastify.register(plugin, { prefix })` and encapsulation | Route files grouped into [modules](modules.md) with explicit `imports`; `apiVersion("v1", routes)` for `/v1` ([API versions](routes.md#api-versions)) |
| `fastify-plugin` to share decorators | Not needed: modules export plain functions in `provides`, called directly |
| `fastify.decorate("db", ...)`, `decorateRequest` | Import the value, or use `ctx.db`, `ctx.ai`, `ctx.jobs` and `state` from middleware |
| Hooks: `onRequest`, `preHandler` for auth and checks | The route's `auth`, `permission` and `rateLimit` options; `createApp({ middleware })` for cross-cutting code |
| Hooks: `onSend`, `onResponse`, `onError` | `createApp({ middleware })` (it sees the response), request logs with timing, and logged errors |
| `fastify.setErrorHandler`, `setNotFoundHandler` | Built in: every error becomes the standard error body; unexpected errors are logged with secrets redacted |
| `@fastify/jwt`, `@fastify/auth`, `@fastify/basic-auth` | `createApp({ auth })` with `bearer(...)` or `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }` ([auth](auth.md)) |
| `@fastify/cors` | `createApp({ cors: { origin: [...] } })` |
| `@fastify/helmet` | Built in: security headers on every response ([security](security.md)) |
| `@fastify/rate-limit` | The route's `rateLimit: { max, per, by }`, with memory or Postgres stores ([routes](routes.md)) |
| `@fastify/formbody`, `bodyLimit` | Built in for JSON and forms, with `createApp({ maxBodySize })` |
| `@fastify/env`, `env-schema` | `config({ schema })` in `src/config.ts` ([configuration](config.md)) |
| `@fastify/swagger`, `@fastify/swagger-ui` | Generated: `GET /openapi.json` from the route schemas |
| `@fastify/under-pressure`, health check plugins | `createApp({ health: true })` with `/health` and `/ready` ([observability](observability.md)) |
| `fastify-metrics` | `createApp({ metrics })` with `/metrics` in the Prometheus format |
| Pino logger, `request.log`, `genReqId` | `createApp({ logging: { format: "json", requests: true } })` and `X-Request-Id` ([observability](observability.md)) |
| `@fastify/schedule`, queue plugins | `job(...)`, `cron(...)` and `inferlo worker` ([jobs](jobs.md)) |
| `reply.sse(...)`, streaming replies | `return ctx.ai.stream(...).toResponse()` for model output, or a `Response` with a `ReadableStream` |
| `fastify.inject()` in tests | `app.request(path, { method, json, as: user })` with a signed-in test user ([testing](testing.md)) |
| `fastify.listen()` and `fastify.close()` | `app.listen(3000)` and `app.close()` on SIGTERM ([deployment](deploy.md)) |

`@fastify/static`, `@fastify/view`, `@fastify/multipart`, `@fastify/websocket` and `@fastify/session` have no Inferlo equivalent yet: keep those routes in Fastify (they keep working next to Inferlo), or serve static files from a CDN or reverse proxy.

## 4. Share auth between both

During the migration, Fastify and Inferlo routes must accept the same credentials. Put the check in one function and use it from both:

```ts
// src/auth-check.ts
export async function userFromToken(token: string | undefined) {
  if (!token) return null;
  const session = await sessions.findByToken(token); // your existing lookup
  return session ? { id: session.userId, roles: session.roles } : null;
}
```

```ts
// Fastify preHandler hook, as before
export async function requireUser(request: FastifyRequest, reply: FastifyReply) {
  const user = await userFromToken(request.headers.authorization?.replace(/^Bearer /, ""));
  if (!user) return reply.code(401).send({ message: "Sign in required" });
  request.user = user;
}
```

```ts
// src/inferlo/auth.ts
import { bearer } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { userFromToken } from "../auth-check.ts";

export const auth = bearer((token) => userFromToken(token));
```

A user needs an `id`, and `roles` for role-based routes. For cookie sessions or other schemes, write `auth: { resolve(req) { ... } }`; `req` is a standard `Request` with the same headers and cookies Fastify sees.

## 5. Keep your data layer, then adopt models where they fit

Inferlo handlers can call any database code you already have (`@fastify/postgres`'s pool, Knex, Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM, MikroORM): import it and use it in the handler. Values that only exist as Fastify decorators (`fastify.pg`) need to be created in a module both sides import, for example a shared `pg` pool. You do not have to move data access to switch routes.

For new tables, use Inferlo [models](database.md): validated inserts and updates, typed queries, relations, pagination and generated migrations (`inferlo db migrate`). Inferlo models expect a `uuid` `id`, `created_at` and `updated_at` columns and snake_case column names, so existing tables that differ are best left with your current code.

## 6. Move the tests

```ts
// Before: fastify.inject with a token
const res = await fastify.inject({ method: "POST", url: "/tickets", headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }, payload: { title: "Printer" } });

// After: signed in as a test user, without a server
import { readJson } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/testing";

const res = await app.request("/tickets", { method: "POST", json: { title: "Printer" }, as: { id: "u1", roles: [] } });
const ticket = await readJson(res, 201);
```

`fastify.inject()` tests keep working during the migration, because moved routes are answered at the same URLs.

## 7. Remove Fastify

When the last Fastify route is gone, start the Inferlo app directly:

```ts
// src/server.ts
import { app } from "./inferlo/app.ts";

const server = await app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000));
console.log(`Listening on http://localhost:${server.port}`);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close({ delayMs: 5000 }));
```

Then remove `fastify` and the plugins Inferlo replaced. Compare your app with a new project from `npx @browserlessapi/inferlo new` for the recommended layout, configuration and AGENTS.md for AI coding tools.

## Checklist

- [ ] `fastify.register(inferloPlugin, { app: inferlo, fallthrough: true })`
- [ ] One auth check shared by Fastify and Inferlo
- [ ] Each moved route: schemas for its input, the right `auth`, `status(201)` where clients expect it, the Fastify route deleted, a test with `app.request`
- [ ] CORS and security headers configured in `createApp` for Inferlo's routes (Fastify's `onSend` plugins do not touch them)
- [ ] Clients told about the new error format, if they read error bodies
- [ ] Fastify removed, `app.listen()` and `app.close()` on SIGTERM

If you only want Inferlo's AI features inside Fastify and no migration, use `fastify.ai` and `request.ai` from [`@browserlessapi/inferlo/fastify`](integrations.md#fastify-1) instead.

---

# Security

Inferlo is secure by default: what you do not turn on stays closed. This page lists the defaults and how to change them.

## Defaults

- **Routes are private.** Every route needs a signed-in user unless it says `auth: "public"`; `auth: "admin"` also checks the role (see [auth](auth.md)). An app with private routes and no `auth` does not start (IL3003).
- **Input is validated.** `body`, `query` and `params` are checked against their `t.*` schemas before the handler runs (IL1001), and unknown fields are removed from bodies.
- **Database values are parameterised.** `db.<table>` methods never build SQL from strings, and every insert and update is validated against the model.
- **Request bodies are limited** to 1 MiB (`createApp({ maxBodySize })`, IL2004).
- **Requests have a time limit** of 60 seconds (`createApp({ requestTimeoutMs })`, per route `timeoutMs`, IL2007), so slow clients and stuck handlers do not hold the server (below).
- **Errors do not leak.** Unexpected errors answer `500` with IL9000 and `"Internal server error"`; the real error is logged. Readiness checks show `"Check failed."`.
- **Secrets stay out of logs.** Authorization and cookie headers, tokens, API keys, passwords in URLs, the AI provider keys and your `config({ secrets })` are replaced with `"[redacted]"` in everything the app logs (below).
- **Cookie sessions resist CSRF.** `sessions()` cookies are signed, `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax`, and requests that change data with a session cookie must send the session's CSRF token (IL3005); see [Cookie sessions](auth.md#cookie-sessions).
- **Single sign-on is checked end to end.** `oidc()` uses the authorization code flow with PKCE, a one-time state and nonce, and checks the ID token's signature, issuer, audience and expiry before it starts a session; `returnTo` can only point at the app. Signing out (`POST /auth/logout`) needs the session's CSRF token and sends the ID token only to the provider that issued it. See [Single sign-on](auth.md#single-sign-on-with-openid-connect).
- **Access tokens are fully checked.** `jwt({ issuer, audience })` requires the audience, checks the signature with the issuer's keys and the expiry, and never accepts `none` or an algorithm that does not match the key; see [Access tokens](auth.md#access-tokens-from-an-identity-provider-jwt).
- **Security headers** are sent on every response (below).
- **Rate limits** are one option away: `rateLimit: { max, per, by }` on a route (see [routes](routes.md)).
- **WebSockets only accept their own origin.** A `route.ws` socket may only be opened from the app's own origin or one listed in `cors.origin` (IL3006), because browsers send cookies with WebSocket upgrades from any page; each message is validated and limited like a request (see [WebSockets](websockets.md)).

## Security headers

Every response gets these headers unless it sets them itself:

| Header | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'` | Pages load scripts, styles and images only from your own origin, and cannot be framed |
| `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` | `same-origin` | Other sites' windows cannot keep a reference to yours |
| `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` | `same-origin` | Other sites cannot embed your responses with `<img>` or `<script>` (CORS requests still work with `cors`) |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `no-referrer` | URLs with tokens or ids are not sent to other sites |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` | Browsers use HTTPS for a year. Only sent over HTTPS (with `trustProxy: true`, also when `X-Forwarded-Proto` is `https`) |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | Browsers do not guess content types |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` | No framing, for older browsers |

They are added to every response: routes, errors, 404s, CORS preflights, health endpoints, OpenAPI, MCP, and responses returned by middleware. A header your handler or middleware sets wins, so a route that serves an HTML page can send its own `Content-Security-Policy`.

Change a header by name (any case), leave one out with `false`, or add your own:

```ts
export const app = createApp({
  // ...
  secureHeaders: {
    "Content-Security-Policy": "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com",
    "X-Frame-Options": "SAMEORIGIN",
    "Strict-Transport-Security": "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload",
    "Permissions-Policy": "camera=(), microphone=()",
    "Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy": false,
  },
});
```

`secureHeaders: false` sends none of them, for example when a proxy in front of the app already adds them. Invalid values (not a string or `false`, line breaks, an invalid header name) raise IL6016. `inferlo describe --json` lists the headers that are sent under `secureHeaders`.

## Request timeouts

Every route has 60 seconds to read its body and run its handler. After that it answers `503` with IL2007 (`"The request took longer than 60000 ms."`), and the request's `ctx.signal` is aborted:

- model calls through `ctx.ai` (`generate`, `stream`, `embed`, including tool rounds) are cancelled, so a stuck provider call stops costing money;
- new `ctx.db` queries fail with IL2007 instead of running (a query already running finishes; put writes that belong together in `db.$transaction`, which then rolls back);
- reading a slow request body stops.

JavaScript cannot stop a running function, so the handler itself keeps going until its next `await` on something that uses the signal; its result is dropped. Pass `ctx.signal` to your own slow work:

```ts
export const importFeed = route
  .post("/feeds/import", { body: Feed, timeoutMs: 120_000 })   // this route may take 2 minutes
  .handle(async ({ body, signal }) => {
    const res = await fetch(body.url, { signal });
    // ...
  });
```

Change the default with `createApp({ requestTimeoutMs: 30_000 })`, give a route its own limit with `timeoutMs`, and turn the limit off with `false` (app-wide or per route), for example for a route that you know streams for a long time. The limit ends when the handler returns: a streamed response (`ai.stream(...).toResponse()`) can keep streaming after it. `ctx.signal` is also aborted when the client disconnects, which cancels `ctx.ai` calls, but not `ctx.db` queries, so a disconnect never leaves half-written data. Invalid values raise IL6017 at startup. `inferlo describe --json` shows `requestTimeoutMs` and each route's own `timeoutMs`.

Tool calls (`ai.generate({ tools })`) and MCP calls run each route with its own limit.

## Secrets in logs

Everything an Inferlo app logs (failed requests, failed jobs, readiness checks, shutdown) goes through a redactor before it reaches your `logger` or the console, and so do error messages shown with `exposeErrors`. It replaces with `"[redacted]"`:

- header values of `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Set-Cookie`, `X-Api-Key` and `Api-Key`, also inside error text and JSON (`Authorization: Bearer [redacted]`), and `Bearer` or `Basic` credentials anywhere;
- passwords in URLs and connection strings (`postgres://app:[redacted]@db:5432/app`) and secrets in query strings (`?key=`, `token=`, `access_token=`, `api_key=`, `password=`, `signature=`);
- common API key formats (`sk-...` for OpenAI and Anthropic, `AIza...` for Google, GitHub tokens);
- the API keys of the app's AI providers (`anthropic({ apiKey })`, `openai`, `gemini`, `openaiCompatible`), even when a provider echoes one back in an error;
- the values you pass to `createApp({ redact })`: your `config()` result (the values of its `secrets`) and any other strings;
- in logged objects, values under keys such as `authorization`, `cookie`, `password`, `secret`, `token`, `apiKey`, `accessToken`, `clientSecret` and `privateKey`.

```ts
import { settings } from "./config.ts";

export const app = createApp({
  // ...
  redact: [settings, process.env.LEGACY_WEBHOOK_SECRET],
});
```

Logged errors stay errors (same class, `code`, `status` and `cause`, with redacted `message` and `stack`), so a custom `logger` can still read them; the originals are not changed. `undefined` and empty values in `redact` are skipped (an unset optional variable); anything that is not a string or a `config()` result raises IL6018. Values shorter than 6 characters are not replaced, because they would hide ordinary text. The standalone `createAI` hides its providers' keys in what it logs too.

## Shutting down

`app.close()` stops taking requests without cutting off the ones in progress; see [graceful shutdown](deploy.md#graceful-shutdown).

---

# Observability

Inferlo gives every request an id, can log every request, writes logs as readable text or as one JSON object per line for log collectors (Datadog, Loki, CloudWatch, Elastic, Google Cloud Logging), serves Prometheus metrics for requests, jobs and AI calls, and traces requests with OpenTelemetry.

```ts
export const app = createApp({
  routes: [tickets],
  logging: { format: "json", requests: true },
  metrics: { token: settings.METRICS_TOKEN },
});
```

## Request ids

Every response has an `X-Request-Id` header, and the same id is:

- `ctx.requestId` in route handlers and `ctx.requestId` in middleware, to pass on to other services or show to users in error pages;
- the `requestId` field of every log entry Inferlo writes for the request (failed requests, `ctx.waitUntil` errors and request logs).

Ids are random UUIDs. Behind a proxy or load balancer that sends its own id, set `createApp({ trustProxy: true })` and Inferlo keeps an incoming `X-Request-Id` header (1 to 128 letters, digits and `.`, `_`, `:`, `-`) so log entries line up across services. Without `trustProxy`, incoming ids are ignored, so clients cannot write into your logs. A handler that sets its own `X-Request-Id` header keeps it.

## Request logs

`logging: { requests: true }` logs one entry per request when its response is ready:

```
[inferlo] GET /tickets 200 4.2ms (request 0b7f8a52-3c1e-4d0a-9a51-8f2f0e6c1d44)
```

The entry's fields are `requestId`, `method`, `path` (without the query string, which can hold secrets), `status` and `durationMs` (time until the response headers were ready; a streamed body can take longer). The health endpoints (`/health` and `/ready`, see [Deployment](deploy.md#health-and-readiness)) are not logged, because load balancers call them every few seconds. Request logs are off by default; new projects turn them on.

## JSON logs

`logging: { format: "json" }` makes the built-in logger write one JSON object per line, info entries to stdout and errors to stderr:

```json
{"time":"2026-11-04T18:20:31.004Z","level":"info","app":"helpdesk","msg":"GET /tickets 200 4.2ms","requestId":"0b7f8a52-3c1e-4d0a-9a51-8f2f0e6c1d44","method":"GET","path":"/tickets","status":200,"durationMs":4.2}
{"time":"2026-11-04T18:20:32.118Z","level":"error","app":"helpdesk","msg":"POST /tickets failed","requestId":"6d1c...","error":{"name":"Error","message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432","code":"ECONNREFUSED","stack":"..."}}
```

- `time`, `level` (`info` or `error`), `app` (`createApp({ name })`) and `msg` are always there, followed by the entry's fields.
- Errors become `error: { name, message, code, status, stack, cause }`; other data is under `data`.
- Like every log entry, JSON lines go through [secret redaction](security.md#secrets-in-logs) first: authorization headers, cookies, tokens, passwords in URLs, provider API keys and your `redact` values are replaced with `"[redacted]"`.

The default is `format: "text"`, which is easier to read in a terminal. A common setup reads the format from configuration:

```ts
// src/config.ts: LOG_FORMAT: t.enum(["text", "json"]).default("text")
createApp({ logging: { format: settings.LOG_FORMAT, requests: true } });
```

## Your own logger

Pass `logger` to send entries to winston, a log library of your company or anything else. Each method gets the message, optional data (an error or a value) and optional `fields` with structured values such as `requestId`:

```ts
createApp({
  logger: {
    info: (message, data, fields) => log.info(message, { ...fields, data }),
    error: (message, data, fields) => log.error(message, { ...fields, error: data }),
  },
  logging: { requests: true },
});
```

Entries are redacted before they reach your logger. `format` only applies to the built-in logger, so passing it together with `logger` raises IL6019; `requests` works with both.

### Pino

Apps that log with [pino](https://getpino.io) (Fastify's and NestJS's usual logger) wrap it with `pinoLogger` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/pino`, so Inferlo's request, error, job and readiness logs land in the same stream as the app's own:

```ts
import pino from "pino";
import { createApp } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { pinoLogger } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/pino";

export const log = pino({ base: { service: "helpdesk" } });

export const app = createApp({
  routes: [tickets],
  logger: pinoLogger(log),
  logging: { requests: true },
});
```

```json
{"level":30,"time":1794083631004,"service":"helpdesk","requestId":"0b7f8a52-3c1e-4d0a-9a51-8f2f0e6c1d44","method":"GET","path":"/tickets","status":200,"durationMs":4.2,"msg":"GET /tickets 200 4.2ms"}
{"level":50,"time":1794083632118,"service":"helpdesk","requestId":"6d1c...","err":{"type":"Error","message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.0.5:5432","stack":"..."},"msg":"POST /tickets failed"}
```

- Each entry is written with `log.info(fields, message)` or `log.error(fields, message)`: fields such as `requestId`, `traceId` and `spanId` (with [tracing](#tracing-opentelemetry)), `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` are top-level properties, an error is `err` (pino's error serializer writes its type, message, stack and cause), and other data is under `data` (for example `data.id` and `data.error` of a failed job).
- Inferlo's [secret redaction](security.md#secrets-in-logs) runs first, and pino's own options (`level`, `base`, `redact`, transports such as `pino-pretty`) still apply.
- Inside Fastify, `pinoLogger(fastify.log)` writes to Fastify's logger. In NestJS with `nestjs-pino`, pass the same pino instance you give `LoggerModule`.
- Passing a pino logger to `logger` without `pinoLogger` raises IL6053, because pino reads `(object, message)` and the request id and error would be lost. `pinoLogger` of anything that is not a logger raises IL6052.
- pino is not a dependency of Inferlo; pino 9.14 and later work (tested on 9.14.0 and the latest release).

`describe().logging` shows the setup (`{ format: "text" | "json" | "custom", requests }`), and `inferlo describe` prints it.

## Error tracking (Sentry)

`onError` is called with every unexpected error after it is logged: answers with a 5xx status (an exception in a handler or middleware, a database error, a failed AI call, a request timeout), failed WebSocket messages and failed job attempts. Client errors (4xx: validation, auth, not found) are not reported. The error is redacted first, like log entries, and the second argument says where it happened:

```ts
createApp({
  onError: (error, info) => tracker.report(error, info),
});
// info: { source: "request", requestId, method, path, route: "/tickets/:id", userId, tenantId, traceId, spanId }
//    or { source: "websocket", requestId, method, path, route, userId, tenantId }
//    or { source: "job", job: "sync-crm", jobId, attempt, maxAttempts, final, tenantId, traceId }
```

Fields that do not apply are left out. `final` is `true` when a job will not be tried again. A hook that throws or rejects is logged ("createApp({ onError }) failed") and never changes the answer or the job's outcome; the hook is not awaited. `onError` that is not a function raises IL6055.

For [Sentry](https://sentry.io), pass `sentryOnError(Sentry)` from `@browserlessapi/inferlo/sentry`:

```ts
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";
import { sentryOnError } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/sentry";

Sentry.init({ dsn: settings.SENTRY_DSN, environment: settings.NODE_ENV });

export const app = createApp({
  routes: [tickets],
  jobs: [jobs],
  onError: sentryOnError(Sentry),
});
```

- Each error is sent with `Sentry.captureException` and the tags `inferlo.source`, `inferlo.route`, `inferlo.job`, `inferlo.final`, `request_id`, `tenant_id` and `trace_id` (when present), so issues can be searched and grouped by route, job or tenant, and a request id from a support ticket finds its error.
- `user` is `{ id }` of the signed-in user only; the email and name are never sent. The `inferlo` context holds every field of `info`.
- Secrets are redacted before Sentry sees the error (authorization headers, tokens, passwords in URLs, provider API keys and your `redact` values); Sentry's own `beforeSend` and data scrubbing still apply.
- Any Sentry SDK with `captureException(error, captureContext)` works: `@sentry/node`, `@sentry/bun`, `@sentry/deno`, `@sentry/cloudflare`, `@sentry/nextjs`. Sentry is not a dependency of Inferlo; `@sentry/node` 9 and later are tested (9.0.0 and the latest). Anything else raises IL6056.

## Metrics

`metrics: true` serves `GET /metrics` in the Prometheus text format, which Prometheus, Grafana Agent and Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Datadog and most other monitoring tools read:

```ts
// src/config.ts: METRICS_TOKEN: t.string().min(16), and "METRICS_TOKEN" in secrets
createApp({ metrics: { token: settings.METRICS_TOKEN } });
```

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: helpdesk
    bearer_token: "<the METRICS_TOKEN value>"
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["helpdesk:3000"]
```

Options:

- `token`: the endpoint answers `401` (IL3001) unless the request sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Use a random secret of at least 16 characters from configuration. `{ token: undefined }` (an unset variable) raises IL6020 instead of making the endpoint public. Without `token` the endpoint is public, like `/health`, so only leave it out when the port is not reachable from the internet (for example a Kubernetes pod scraped inside the cluster).
- `path`: default `"/metrics"`. It cannot be the OpenAPI, MCP or health path or a `GET` route.
- `buckets`: upper bounds in seconds for the duration histograms. Default `[0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10]`.

Invalid options raise IL6020. Metrics are off by default; new projects turn them on when `METRICS_TOKEN` is set. `describe().endpoints.metrics` shows the path (or `false`).

### What is measured

| Metric | Type | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| `inferlo_info` | gauge (always 1) | `app`, `version` (`createApp({ name, version })`), `inferlo` |
| `inferlo_http_requests_total` | counter | `method`, `route`, `status` |
| `inferlo_http_request_duration_seconds` | histogram | `method`, `route` |
| `inferlo_http_requests_in_flight` | gauge | |
| `inferlo_job_runs_total` | counter | `job`, `outcome` (`done`, `retried` or `failed`) |
| `inferlo_job_duration_seconds` | histogram | `job` |
| `inferlo_ai_calls_total` | counter | `requested` (the alias or model you asked for), `model` (the `provider:model` that answered), `kind` (`generate`, `stream` or `embed`) |
| `inferlo_ai_tokens_total` | counter | `requested`, `model`, `type` (`input` or `output`) |
| `inferlo_ai_cost_usd_total` | counter | `requested`, `model` (from `ai.pricing`; 0 without prices) |
| `inferlo_ai_call_duration_seconds` | histogram | `requested`, `model` |

- `route` is the route pattern (`/tickets/:id`), never the path with ids in it, so the number of series stays small. It is the OpenAPI or MCP path for those endpoints, and `unmatched` for `404` and `405` answers and responses sent by middleware without calling `next()`.
- Methods other than `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` and `OPTIONS` are counted as `OTHER`, so clients cannot create new series.
- Durations are measured until the response headers are ready, like request logs; a streamed body can take longer.
- The health endpoints and the metrics endpoint itself are not counted.
- AI metrics count every call that reports usage (the same calls as `ai.onUsage`, which still runs), whether it came from `ctx.ai` in a route, a job or `app.ai`. Calls of a separate `createAI(...)` client are not counted.
- Job metrics count attempts run by this process (`app.jobs.start()` or `app.jobs.runDue()`). Each instance has its own counters; Prometheus adds them up across instances with `sum(...)`.

Useful queries:

```
# Requests per second by route, and the share of 5xx answers
sum by (route) (rate(inferlo_http_requests_total[5m]))
sum(rate(inferlo_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(inferlo_http_requests_total[5m]))

# 95th percentile latency by route
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, route) (rate(inferlo_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

# AI spend per alias in the last day, and failed jobs
sum by (requested) (increase(inferlo_ai_cost_usd_total[1d]))
sum by (job) (increase(inferlo_job_runs_total{outcome="failed"}[1h]))
```

## Tracing (OpenTelemetry)

Pass the OpenTelemetry API you already use, and every request gets a server span:

```ts
import * as otel from "@opentelemetry/api";

export const app = createApp({
  routes: [tickets],
  tracing: { api: otel },
});
```

Inferlo has no dependency on OpenTelemetry (`@opentelemetry/api` 1.3 and newer is an optional peer dependency): it uses the API you pass, so spans go wherever the OpenTelemetry SDK you start exports them (an OTLP collector, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog). Start the SDK before the app, for example `node --import ./otel.ts src/server.ts` with `@opentelemetry/sdk-node`. Without an SDK, the API's no-op tracer is used and nothing is recorded.

- **One server span per request**, named after the matched route (`GET /tickets/:id`; requests that match no route keep just the method, so names stay few), with the attributes `http.request.method`, `http.route`, `http.response.status_code`, `url.path`, `url.scheme`, `server.address`, `server.port` and `user_agent.original`. Answers with status 500 or more set the span's status to error and record the exception; 4xx answers do not. The span ends when the response headers are ready (a streamed body can take longer).
- **It continues the caller's trace**: the incoming `traceparent` header (and whatever else the propagator your SDK registers reads) becomes the span's parent, so a trace runs through every service.
- **The handler runs inside the span**: spans you start with `otel.trace.getTracer(...)` and spans from instrumentations (outgoing `fetch`, `pg`) become its children, and `otel.trace.getActiveSpan()` returns it.
- **Logs carry the trace**: every log entry Inferlo writes for the request (request logs, failed requests) gets `traceId` and `spanId` fields next to `requestId`, so your log tool links logs and traces.
- The health, readiness and metrics endpoints are not traced. The tracer is named after the app (`createApp({ name })`) with its `version`; set `tracing: { api: otel, tracerName: "billing-api" }` to change it.
- Anything else than `{ api }` with the OpenTelemetry API raises IL6030 at startup.

### AI calls

Every `ai.generate`, `ai.stream` and `ai.embed` call gets a client span under the active span (the request's, or yours), following the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions:

| Attribute | Example |
|---|---|
| span name | `chat claude-haiku-4-5`, `embeddings text-embedding-3-small` (operation and the first model of the alias) |
| `gen_ai.operation.name` | `chat` or `embeddings` |
| `gen_ai.provider.name` | `anthropic` (the provider that answered) |
| `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.model` | the first model of the alias, and the model that answered (they differ after a fallback) |
| `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens` | token counts of the whole call, tool steps included |
| `gen_ai.request.max_tokens`, `gen_ai.request.temperature` | when you set them |
| `inferlo.ai.model` | the alias you asked for (`fast`) |
| `inferlo.ai.cost_usd` | cost from `pricing` (0 without pricing) |
| `inferlo.ai.steps` | model calls in `generate` (more than 1 with tools or repairs) |
| `inferlo.ai.stream`, `inferlo.ai.cancelled` | `true` for streams, and when the reader stopped early |

- Prompts, answers, tool inputs and the `for` user id are never recorded.
- The span is active while `generate` runs, so routes and function tools the model calls, and their database queries, become its children. A stream's span ends when the stream does.
- A failed call (for example when every model failed) sets the error status, records the exception and sets `error.type` to the Inferlo error code (`IL5003`).
- `createAI` on its own (`@browserlessapi/inferlo/ai`, in any framework) takes the same option: `createAI({ providers, models, tracing: { api: otel } })`. In an app, `createApp({ tracing })` turns it on for `ctx.ai` and `app.ai`.
- Calls to other services with `serviceClient({ ..., tracing: { api: otel } })` get a client span per attempt and send its `traceparent`, so the receiving service's spans join the same trace. See [Tracing across services](services.md#tracing-across-services).

### Database queries

Queries made while a request or job is traced get a client span named after the operation and table (`SELECT tickets`, `INSERT audit_log`) with `db.system.name` (`postgresql`), `db.operation.name` and `db.collection.name`. Raw SQL (`db.$sql`) and Inferlo's own queries (rate limits, cache, job queue) get a span named after the statement (`UPDATE`) with the parameterised SQL in `db.query.text`. Values are never recorded. Queries outside a trace, such as startup or the worker polling for jobs, are not traced, so idle instances send no spans. If you also use the `pg` instrumentation, its spans appear as children of these.

### Jobs

A job continues the trace it was enqueued in. `ctx.jobs.enqueue(...)` in a traced request (or job) stores the trace with the job (W3C `traceparent` and `tracestate`, in the `trace` field of the job record and in the `inferlo_jobs` table with the database queue), and every attempt runs in a consumer span `process send-email` whose parent is that request's span, even when another instance runs it hours later. The span is active while the handler runs, so the job's database queries and AI calls are its children.

| Attribute | Example |
|---|---|
| `messaging.system`, `messaging.operation.type` | `inferlo`, `process` |
| `messaging.destination.name` | the job name |
| `messaging.message.id` | the job id (`app.jobs.get(id)`) |
| `inferlo.job.attempt` | 1 for the first run, 2 for the first retry |
| `inferlo.job.outcome` | `done`, `retried` or `failed` |

A failed attempt sets the error status, records the exception and sets `error.type` (the Inferlo error code, or the error's name). Jobs enqueued outside a trace, such as cron ticks or `app.jobs.enqueue` in a script, start a new trace. The database queue adds the `traceparent` and `tracestate` columns to an existing `inferlo_jobs` table by itself.

---

# Deployment

An Inferlo app is a standard `fetch(Request) => Response` handler, so it runs anywhere.

## Linux server (Node.js)

```bash
npm ci --omit=dev
DATABASE_URL=postgres://... npx inferlo db migrate --apply   # or inferlo db push if you do not use migrations
DATABASE_URL=postgres://... PORT=3000 node src/server.ts
```

Run it under systemd or pm2 behind Nginx:

```nginx
location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_buffering off;   # needed for AI streaming responses
}
```

Behind a proxy like this, set `createApp({ trustProxy: true })` so routes with `rateLimit: { by: "ip" }` see the client's address instead of the proxy's. With more than one instance, use `rateLimit: { store: "database" }` (or `"redis"`, see [Redis](redis.md)) so the counts are shared, and `jobQueue: { store: "database" }` (or `"redis"`) so background jobs are too (see [jobs](jobs.md)).

## Health and readiness

Load balancers, Kubernetes and other orchestrators ask two questions: is the process alive, and can it take traffic? `createApp({ health: true })` answers both:

```ts
export const app = createApp({
  // ...
  health: {
    checks: { search: () => search.ping() },   // optional: your own dependencies
  },
});
```

- `GET /health` (liveness) answers `200 {"status":"ok"}` while the process can answer requests. It runs no checks, so a slow database never gets a healthy instance restarted.
- `GET /ready` (readiness) runs every check at the same time and answers `200` when all pass, `503` when any fails:

```json
{ "status": "not_ready", "checks": { "database": { "status": "ok", "durationMs": 2 }, "ai": { "status": "ok", "durationMs": 0 }, "search": { "status": "error", "durationMs": 5000, "error": "Timed out after 5000 ms." } } }
```

Built-in checks: `database` runs `select 1` on Postgres (which also covers `rateLimit` and `jobQueue` with `store: "database"`; the memory database is always ready), `redis` (with `createApp({ redis })`) sends `PING` to Redis, and `ai` (when AI is configured) checks that every alias points to a configured provider. It does not call the models, so readiness probes cost nothing. A check passes when it returns or resolves, and fails when it throws, rejects or takes longer than `timeoutMs` (default 5000).

Both endpoints are public, send `Cache-Control: no-store` and also answer `HEAD`. Failed checks show `"Check failed."` and the real error is logged, so connection strings and hostnames never reach the response; throw `httpError(503, "Replica lag too high")` to show your own message, or set `exposeErrors: true` in development. Change the paths with `health: { path: "/livez", readyPath: "/readyz" }`. `await app.checkReady()` returns the same report in code (for example in a startup script), and `inferlo describe` lists the endpoints. Invalid options, or a route that uses the same path, raise IL6014.

Kubernetes:

```yaml
livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /health, port: 3000 } }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 3000 }, periodSeconds: 10 }
```

For dashboards and alerts, `createApp({ metrics: { token } })` serves Prometheus metrics at `GET /metrics` (requests, jobs, AI calls, tokens and cost); see [metrics](observability.md#metrics).

## Graceful shutdown

When an instance is stopped (a deploy, scaling down, a node drain), the orchestrator sends SIGTERM and waits a grace period before it kills the process. `app.close()` uses that time so no request or job is cut off:

```ts
// src/server.ts (new projects do this)
const server = await app.listen(settings.PORT);
app.jobs.start();
process.on("SIGTERM", () => void app.close({ delayMs: 5000 }));
```

In order:

1. `app.closing` becomes `true` and `GET /ready` answers `503` with `{ "status": "not_ready", "checks": { "shutdown": { "status": "error", "durationMs": 0, "error": "The app is shutting down." } } }`, so load balancers stop sending traffic. `GET /health` keeps answering `200`, so the instance is not restarted.
2. For `delayMs` (default 0) requests are still served. Set it a little longer than the readiness probe period plus the time your load balancer needs to remove the instance (5 to 10 seconds is common on Kubernetes).
3. New requests then get `503` with code IL2006 and `Connection: close`, so clients and proxies retry on another instance.
4. In-flight requests, `ctx.waitUntil` tasks and the job workers started with `app.jobs.start()` (with their running job) finish, for at most `timeoutMs` (default 10000). If they take longer, `app.close()` logs what was still running and goes on.
5. Servers started with `app.listen()` close (open connections are closed when the time is up), then the database.

Calling `app.close()` again returns the same promise. Keep `delayMs + timeoutMs` below the orchestrator's grace period (30 seconds on Kubernetes by default). A request counts as in flight until its handler returns; a streamed response that is still sending when the time is up is cut off when the server closes. Invalid options raise IL6015. `inferlo worker` shuts down the same way for jobs: it stops taking jobs on SIGTERM and waits for the running one.

## Bun

```bash
bun src/server.ts
```

`app.listen()` uses `Bun.serve` automatically, with the client address from Bun's `server.requestIP()` for rate limits by IP. `app.close()` (see [graceful shutdown](#graceful-shutdown)) lets requests and streamed answers that are still running finish, then stops the server and closes its keep-alive connections; when `timeoutMs` is up, it closes the connections that are still open.

To serve Bun's own routes (static files, HTML imports of a full-stack app) from the same server, use `Bun.serve` yourself with the Inferlo app as the `fetch` handler for every other request:

```ts
// src/server.ts
import homepage from "./index.html";
import { app } from "./app.ts";

const server = Bun.serve({
  port: Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000),
  routes: { "/": homepage },   // Bun's routes match first
  fetch: app.fetch,            // everything else: Inferlo routes (/api/...), /health, /ready, OpenAPI and MCP
});
app.jobs.start();

process.on("SIGTERM", async () => {
  await app.close();           // /ready answers 503, new requests get 503 IL2006, waits for running handlers and jobs
  await server.stop();         // stops listening; resolves when the open connections are done
});
```

- Bun passes its server as the second argument of `fetch`, so `app.fetch` gets the client address without a wrapper. Behind a proxy, set `createApp({ trustProxy: true })` so `X-Forwarded-For` is used.
- Inferlo's routes keep their full paths here (`route.get("/api/notes", ...)`): Bun does not remove a prefix. To serve an app whose routes start at `/` under a path, mount it in a framework that does (Hono's `app.mount("/api", inferlo.fetch)`, see [integrations](integrations.md)).
- Streamed AI answers (`ai.stream(...).toResponse()`, server-sent events) are sent as they are generated. Bun closes connections that send nothing for `idleTimeout` seconds (10 by default), so `app.fetch` turns that timeout off for each server-sent events answer (with Bun's `server.timeout(request, 0)`), and a model may pause between tokens for longer. Other long, quiet streams you return yourself follow `idleTimeout`; raise it with `Bun.serve({ idleTimeout: 60, ... })` (at most 255).
- Inferlo is tested on Bun 1.3.0 and the latest Bun, including this setup (test/bun-serve.test.ts).

## Deno

```bash
deno run -A src/server.ts
```

`app.listen()` uses `Deno.serve` automatically, with the client address from Deno's `info.remoteAddr` for rate limits by IP. `app.close()` (see [graceful shutdown](#graceful-shutdown)) lets requests and streamed answers that are still running finish, then shuts the server down; when `timeoutMs` is up, it cuts off the answers that are still streaming.

To start the server yourself, pass `app.fetch` as the handler. Deno passes its handler info as the second argument, so the app gets the client address without a wrapper:

```ts
// src/server.ts
import { app } from "./app.ts";

const server = Deno.serve({ port: Number(Deno.env.get("PORT") ?? 3000) }, app.fetch);
app.jobs.start();

Deno.addSignalListener("SIGTERM", async () => {
  await app.close();           // /ready answers 503, new requests get 503 IL2006, waits for running handlers and jobs
  await server.shutdown();     // stops listening; resolves when the open answers are done
});
```

With `deno serve` (and on Deno Deploy), the module's default export is the server: an Inferlo app has the `fetch` method it needs, so export the app itself.

```ts
// src/main.ts: deno serve -A src/main.ts (add --port to choose the port)
import { app } from "./app.ts";
export default app;
```

- Packages from npm work as on Node.js: `npm:` specifiers, or a `package.json` with `node_modules` (what `inferlo new` creates; Deno reads it). Environment variables reach `config()` and `env()` through Deno's `process.env`, so run with `--allow-env` (or `-A`).
- Streamed AI answers (`ai.stream(...).toResponse()`, server-sent events) are sent as they are generated.
- `ctx.signal` aborts when the client disconnects. Deno 2.9 also aborts a request's signal after its answer was delivered (Deno's legacy behaviour; it prints a notice about it the first time a handler uses the signal), so on Deno work you hand to `ctx.waitUntil` should not depend on `ctx.signal`. Run Deno with `--unstable-no-legacy-abort` to abort it only on disconnect.
- Behind a proxy, set `createApp({ trustProxy: true })` so `X-Forwarded-For` is used.
- Inferlo is tested on Deno 2.9.0 and the latest Deno: the whole test suite and the examples run on Deno in CI with PostgreSQL and Redis, including these setups (test/deno-serve.test.ts).

## Cloudflare Workers and other edge runtimes

```ts
import { app } from "./app.ts";
export default app;   // app.fetch is the Worker handler
```

On Cloudflare Workers, set `"compatibility_flags": ["nodejs_compat"]` and a `compatibility_date` of 2025-04-01 or later in `wrangler.jsonc`, so vars and secrets reach `config()` and `env()`. Deploy with `npx wrangler deploy`. Bindings, the client address, `waitUntil` and AI on Workers are in [Cloudflare Workers](integrations.md#cloudflare-workers). Use `memory()` for stateless services; the Postgres adapter is not yet tested on Workers.

## Vercel and Netlify Functions

```ts
// Vercel: api/index.ts, with vercel.json rewriting every path to /api
import { app } from "../src/app.ts";
export default app;
```

```ts
// Netlify: netlify/functions/api.ts
import { app } from "../../src/app.ts";
export default app.fetch;
export const config = { path: "/api/*" };
```

Rate limits by IP use the address the platform sets (`X-Real-IP` on Vercel, `context.ip` on Netlify), and `ctx.waitUntil` keeps the function alive until the work settles. See [Vercel Functions](integrations.md#vercel-functions) and [Netlify Functions](integrations.md#netlify-functions).

## AWS Lambda

```ts
import { toLambdaHandler } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/lambda";
import { app } from "./app.ts";

export const handler = toLambdaHandler(app);                       // function URLs and API Gateway
// export const handler = toLambdaHandler(app, { streaming: true }); // function URLs with response streaming
```

See [AWS Lambda](integrations.md#aws-lambda) for event formats, cookies, binary bodies and streaming AI answers.

## Azure Functions

```ts
// src/functions/inferlo.ts
import { app as azure } from "@azure/functions";
import { toAzureHandler } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo/azure";
import { app } from "../app.ts";

azure.setup({ enableHttpStream: true });
azure.http("inferlo", {
  route: "{*path}",
  methods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"],
  authLevel: "anonymous",
  handler: toAzureHandler(app, { prefix: "/api" }),
});
```

See [Azure Functions](integrations.md#azure-functions) for the route prefix, cookies, client addresses and streaming AI answers.

## Google Cloud Run functions

```ts
// src/index.ts
import * as functions from "@google-cloud/functions-framework";
import { toNodeHandler } from "@browserlessapi/inferlo";
import { app } from "./app.ts";

functions.http("inferlo", toNodeHandler(app));
```

Deploy with `gcloud run deploy my-api --source . --function inferlo --base-image nodejs22`. See [Google Cloud Run functions](integrations.md#google-cloud-run-functions).

## Inside another framework

To run an Inferlo app under a path of an existing Express, Fastify, NestJS or Hono app, see [Use with other frameworks](integrations.md) (`toNodeHandler(app, { prefix })`).

---

# Performance

Inferlo publishes a reproducible throughput and latency benchmark against Fastify, Hono, Express and NestJS. It lives in `bench/perf/` and runs with one command:

```bash
npm ci
npm run bench:perf                                    # every framework, 10 s per route after a 3 s warm-up
node bench/perf/run.ts --only inferlo,fastify --duration 5 --connections 100
node bench/perf/run.ts --json                         # machine-readable results
```

## What is measured

Every framework serves the same two routes from its own Node.js process (`bench/perf/servers/<framework>.ts`):

| Route | Request | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /hello` | none | `{"hello":"world"}` |
| `POST /echo` | `{"name":"Ada","count":3}` | the body, after checking `name` (1 to 100 characters) and `count` (a whole number from 0 to 1000); an invalid body gets a 4xx |

- Inferlo runs with its defaults, as an app in production would: request ids, secure response headers, schema validation, the request timeout and the error handler are on; request logging and OpenAPI are off. It is served by `app.listen()`.
- Fastify validates the body with its built-in JSON schema support. Hono runs on `@hono/node-server`. Express uses `express.json()`. NestJS uses its default Express platform. Hono, Express and NestJS check the body with the same hand-written function, because they have no built-in validation.
- Before a framework is measured, the runner checks that it answers each route correctly and rejects an invalid body (the test `test/perf-servers.test.ts` does the same in CI), so a broken server cannot look fast.
- The load comes from [autocannon](https://github.com/mcollina/autocannon) in the runner's process: 50 connections, no pipelining, a warm-up run, then the measured run, one framework at a time. It reports the average requests per second and the 99th percentile latency.

## Results

Measured on 2026-11-05 with Inferlo from the main branch after performance part 2a (Fastify 5.12, Hono 4.13, Express 5.3, NestJS 12.3), Node.js 22.23.4 on Linux x64, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz with 2 CPUs; 50 connections, 10 s per route after a 3 s warm-up. The load generator shares the 2 CPUs with the server, so the fastest frameworks are partly limited by it.

| Framework | `GET /hello` req/s | p99 ms | `POST /echo` req/s | p99 ms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Inferlo | 14,306 | 9 | 10,070 | 13 |
| Fastify | 57,727 | 2 | 37,438 | 3 |
| Hono | 60,899 | 2 | 33,337 | 3 |
| Express | 11,706 | 11 | 10,602 | 11 |
| NestJS | 10,593 | 12 | 8,019 | 15 |

Inferlo is at the level of Express and NestJS and behind Fastify and Hono.

### History

| Date | Change | Inferlo `GET /hello` req/s | `POST /echo` req/s |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 2026-11-05 | First measurement (Inferlo 0.6.0) | 11,894 | 8,494 |
| 2026-11-05 | Part 2a: `ctx.signal`, `ctx.ai` and `ctx.audit` built on first use; the client's disconnect signal kept next to the Request instead of inside it; JSON answers written in one piece with `Content-Length` | 14,306 | 10,070 |

Each row was measured on the machine above, in the same run as the other frameworks. What is left, from CPU profiles: building a full Web `Request` and `Headers` for every Node.js request, reading the body through a Web stream, and garbage collection of those objects. Closing that gap is on the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md) (performance part 2b). This page is updated with every new measurement.

## Regression check in CI

Every push runs `npm run bench:perf:check` (bench/perf/check.ts) in the "Performance regression check" CI job. It measures Inferlo and Fastify on both routes in three rounds (5 s per route after a 2 s warm-up) and fails when Inferlo's throughput **relative to Fastify's** drops below the floor for a route in `bench/perf/limits.json`:

```json
{ "minRatio": { "GET /hello (JSON)": 0.15, "POST /echo (validated JSON body)": 0.15 } }
```

- Absolute requests per second depend on the runner, so they are never compared: both frameworks run on the same machine in the same run, and the speed of the runner cancels out.
- Each round gives one Inferlo / Fastify ratio per route, and the check uses the median, so one noisy round does not decide the result. Errors or non-2xx answers under load fail the check.
- A floor is only ever raised: when a change makes Inferlo faster, raise the floor (leaving room for runner noise, about a quarter below the ratios CI reports) so the gain is kept. A change that falls below a floor is profiled and made faster, not merged with a lower floor.

The first floors are 0.15 for both routes, below the 0.26 to 0.36 measured on the machine above, while CI collects the ratios of its own runners; they are raised once those are known.

Run it locally with `npm run bench:perf:check`, or `node bench/perf/check.ts --rounds 5 --duration 10` for a steadier result.

Numbers depend on the machine, the Node.js version and the load. Compare frameworks within one run, and run the benchmark on hardware like your production servers before drawing conclusions.

---

# Support policy

This page says which Inferlo versions get fixes, how versions are numbered, how features are deprecated and removed, and which runtimes, databases and frameworks each release supports. It applies to the npm package `@browserlessapi/inferlo` and all of its entry points (`/ai`, `/postgres`, `/testing` and the framework integrations).

## Versions

Inferlo follows [semantic versioning](https://semver.org): `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.

| Change | Before 1.0 (now) | From 1.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Bug and security fixes | patch (`0.4.1`) | patch (`1.2.1`) |
| New features, backwards compatible | minor (`0.5.0`) | minor (`1.3.0`) |
| Breaking changes | minor (`0.5.0`), always listed under "Breaking" in the [changelog](../CHANGELOG.md) | major only (`2.0.0`) |

What counts as public API, and therefore as breaking when it changes:

- everything exported from the package's entry points, and the documented behaviour of those exports;
- error codes (`ILxxxx`): a code is never reused or given another meaning, and the `code`, `status` and JSON shape of errors stay the same;
- the CLI's commands, flags and `--json` output;
- the HTTP behaviour of an app: status codes, response shapes, default headers, `/health`, `/ready`, `/openapi.json` and `/mcp`;
- files Inferlo writes and reads: migration files, `migrations/snapshot.json` and the tables `inferlo_migrations`, `inferlo_jobs` and `inferlo_rate_limits`;
- the supported versions below (dropping one is breaking, except when it reached end of life upstream).

Not public API: anything not exported or documented, the text of error messages (match on `code`), log message text (use the structured `fields`, see [Observability](observability.md)), and the exact format of `inferlo describe` without `--json`.

Releases are published to npm by CI only, with [provenance](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements), and each one has a GitHub release with its changelog entries. While Inferlo is below 1.0, releases go out as often as daily when there are changes.

## Which versions get fixes

Before 1.0 only the latest minor version gets fixes. Upgrade to the latest release to get a fix; the changelog lists every breaking change with how to upgrade.

From 1.0:

| Release line | Bug fixes | Security fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Latest major (`1.x`), latest minor | Yes | Yes |
| Latest major, older minors | No, upgrade within the major (no breaking changes) | No, upgrade within the major |
| Previous major (LTS) | Critical bugs only | Yes, for 12 months after the next major is released |
| Older majors | No | No |

Each new major version keeps the previous one supported for security fixes for 12 months, so teams have a year to upgrade. A major version is released at most once a year.

## Deprecations

Public APIs are never removed or renamed without a deprecation first:

1. The old API keeps working and is marked `@deprecated` in its types (editors and AI coding tools show it), with the replacement named.
2. The changelog entry that deprecates it has a migration note: what to change, with a before and after example.
3. Where possible, using it logs one warning per process naming the replacement.
4. It is removed no earlier than the next major version (before 1.0: no earlier than the next minor version, listed under "Breaking").

Runtime, database and framework versions follow their upstream end of life instead (below).

## Supported runtimes, databases and frameworks

Every version range below is tested in CI on its oldest supported and its latest version, and every PostgreSQL major version still supported upstream is tested. A weekly CI run tests new upstream releases even when Inferlo did not change.

| Component | Supported |
|---|---|
